sense: disturbing because it deals with death or horror
definition: Disturbing because it is concerned with death, decay or horror.
nuance: Macabre describes images, stories, jokes and details that dwell on death in a grim or eerie way. It is common in writing about art, literature, crime and horror. It is not simply 'sad': it suggests something chilling or morbid.

examples.text: Halloween shops sell macabre decorations such as plastic skeletons, coffins and fake gravestones.
Gothic novels often combine romance with macabre imagery of tombs and decaying castles.
Police described the discovery of bones hidden in the cellar as a macabre find.
The old house was full of macabre souvenirs: a stuffed raven, a surgeon's saw and a jar of human teeth.
The museum's collection of preserved specimens holds a macabre fascination for many visitors.
It's a bit macabre, but I love reading about old graveyards and the stories behind them.

cloze.text: Medieval artists painted the 'dance of death', a ___ scene in which skeletons lead people to the grave.
The detective novel opens with a ___ discovery: a row of carefully arranged skulls in a cellar.
There is something ___ about the Victorian habit of photographing dead relatives propped up as if still alive.

misuse.text: We had a macabre picnic in the sunny park, with lemonade and silly games.
misuse.why: Macabre means disturbingly connected with death or horror, so it does not suit a cheerful picnic.

misuse.text: The macabre comedy was gentle, warm and full of happy weddings.
misuse.why: Macabre describes grim, death-related material, the opposite of gentle, happy weddings.

synonyms.vs: Gruesome stresses shocking physical horror; macabre suggests an eerie, chilling interest in death itself.
Grisly is about horrible details of violence or death; macabre adds a sense of the weird or ghostly.
Morbid describes an unhealthy interest in death, often in a person; macabre usually describes things, images or humour.

origin: From the French phrase danse macabre, 'dance of death', a medieval picture of skeletons leading living people to the grave.

definition: Unfair favouritism shown to relatives or close friends, especially by giving them jobs or promotions.
nuance: Nepotism is a critical word for appointing family members in business, politics or institutions regardless of merit. It appears in news stories about scandals and in history essays about courts and dynasties. It suggests unfairness to better-qualified outsiders.

examples.text: The minister was accused of nepotism after appointing his nephew to run the new agency.
Historians link the decline of the dynasty to widespread nepotism, as relatives filled every senior post.
Everyone knows she got the job through nepotism; her uncle owns the company.
The company's code of conduct bans nepotism in hiring and promotion decisions.
In the old family firm, nepotism was simply the way things were done: cousins, in-laws and godsons all drew a salary.
Studies suggest that nepotism can damage morale because talented outsiders see no route to promotion.

cloze.text: Hiring his three cousins without advertising the posts was a clear case of ___, not fair selection.
The university introduced open competitions to end the ___ that had filled departments with the professors' relatives.
Critics say the party is full of ___: jobs go to the relatives of its leaders, whatever their talent.

misuse.text: She was praised for her nepotism after choosing the best candidate from hundreds of applicants.
misuse.why: Nepotism means unfairly favouring relatives, not choosing the best candidate on merit.

misuse.text: Her nepotism towards her nephew showed in the generous birthday presents she sent him every year.
misuse.why: Nepotism is favouring relatives with jobs or power, not ordinary kindness to family such as giving presents.

synonyms.vs: Favouritism is any unfair preference; nepotism is specifically favouring members of your own family.
Cronyism favours friends and political allies; nepotism favours relatives.

origin: From Italian nepotismo, from nepote, 'nephew', because some popes gave important posts to their nephews.

sense: equivalent in effect to something worse
definition: Having the same effect as something else, usually something more serious or unwelcome.
nuance: Tantamount is always followed by 'to' and never comes before a noun. It says that one thing is, in effect, the same as another, usually stronger, thing: 'tantamount to a confession'. It is common in news, law and argument.

examples.text: The president's refusal to answer was tantamount to an admission that the rumours were true.
Some philosophers argue that ignoring the evidence is tantamount to choosing to be wrong.
Telling her you'd 'think about it' was tantamount to saying no.
Under the contract, failure to pay by the deadline is tantamount to a breach.
To walk out in the middle of the speech was tantamount to a declaration of war.
Critics claim that the policy is tantamount to censorship, even though no book is officially banned.

cloze.text: Leaving the scene of the accident without a word is ___ to admitting that you were at fault.
In this industry, ignoring a customer's complaint is ___ to losing that customer for ever.
The senator said the new fee was ___ to a tax rise, although the government insisted it was something else.

misuse.text: The two brothers look tantamount, with the same eyes and the same smile.
misuse.why: Tantamount is used with 'to' for equivalent effect, not to say that people look alike.

misuse.text: A tantamount decision was made at the meeting yesterday.
misuse.why: Tantamount cannot go before a noun; it follows 'is' and needs 'to', as in 'tantamount to a refusal'.

phrases: This is tantamount to saying that...

synonyms.vs: Equivalent is neutral and can go before a noun; tantamount is formal and usually links a mild act to a serious result.
As good as is informal and spoken; tantamount is formal and suits arguments and warnings.

sense: be a perfect example of a kind
definition: To be a perfect example of a kind of thing, showing its main qualities.
nuance: Typify is used when one person, event or object shows clearly what a whole group or period is like. It is common in essays on style, history and society. The subject is the example, and the object is the group it stands for.

examples.text: The small, tightly packed terraced house typifies the housing built for workers in Victorian northern towns.
The scandal typifies the culture of secrecy that critics say has grown inside the bank.
That cafe typifies the area: cheap, noisy and always full of students.
The report cites two cases that typify the problems facing rural clinics.
Her grandfather's careful, stubborn manner typified a generation that never discussed feelings.
Imagist poetry, typified by Ezra Pound's 'In a Station of the Metro', used sharp images and very few words.

cloze.text: A rainy match, a late goal and a heartbroken crowd: that one afternoon seemed to ___ the whole season.
Long hours, low pay and endless forms: her first job seemed to ___ everything that was wrong with the industry.
Thick walls and rounded arches ___ Romanesque churches, while pointed arches belong to the Gothic style.

misuse.text: Impressionism typifies this painting, with its soft light and loose brushstrokes.
misuse.why: The example is the subject: this painting typifies Impressionism, not the other way round.

misuse.text: She typified a long letter on her computer.
misuse.why: Typify is not the same as 'type'; it means to be a perfect example, not to write on a keyboard.

synonyms.vs: Epitomise suggests the very best or purest example; typify is milder and means a good, representative example.
Exemplify often means giving or being an illustration of a point; typify stresses being typical of a whole group or period.
Embody means to express a quality or idea in a visible form; typify shows what is usual in a group.

confusables.note: Personify means to represent an idea as a person, or to embody a quality very strongly.

origin: From type, from Greek typos, 'a mark or impression', plus the ending -ify, 'to make'.

sense: stay in a poor or neglected state
definition: To remain in a poor or neglected state for a long time, without improving or being helped.
nuance: Languish suggests a long, unhappy wait in unwelcome conditions, such as prison, poverty or obscurity. It is used for people and for things like proposals, cases and careers that are stuck. It is usually followed by 'in' or 'at'.

examples.text: The prisoner languished in a damp cell for years, forgotten by everyone outside.
Hundreds of cases languish in the courts for years because there are too few judges.
Many early inventions languished in obscurity until later scientists recognised their value.
My unfinished novel has been languishing in a drawer for three years.
The proposal languished in committee after the funding was withdrawn.
Languishing in poverty, many rural communities were left out of the economic boom.

cloze.text: Instead of thriving, the old factory will ___ for another decade, unused, unloved and slowly rotting away.
Her talented sister ___ in a dull office job for years, never given a chance to use her skills.
The bill has been ___ in parliament for months, neglected and forgotten, with no vote and no debate scheduled.

misuse.text: She languished happily on the beach, enjoying a busy day of swimming and games.
misuse.why: Languish means to stay in a poor or neglected state, not to enjoy yourself actively.

misuse.text: The team languished to the top of the league with ten straight wins.
misuse.why: Languish suggests being stuck in a bad position, so it cannot describe rising to the top.

synonyms.vs: Rot is informal and stronger; languish is formal and can describe neglected people, plans or things.
Stagnate means to stop developing; languish adds the idea of being neglected or suffering.
Wither means to dry up and shrink, often literally; languish describes a long, weak, unhappy state.

confusables.note: Linger means to stay longer than expected, without the sense of suffering or neglect.

origin: From Old French languir, from Latin languere, 'to be weak or faint'.

definition: To praise something or someone very highly and enthusiastically.
nuance: Extol means to give lavish praise, often by listing qualities or benefits. It is common in speeches, reviews, advertising and essays about writers who admire an idea. The object is usually a virtue, a benefit or a person.

examples.text: At the retirement dinner, speaker after speaker extolled her patience, kindness and skill.
The essay extols the virtues of slow reading in an age of constant distraction.
Advertisements extol the benefits of the diet, but doctors remain unconvinced.
My dad is always extolling the joys of getting up at five in the morning.
The old sailor extolled the beauty of the sea until the whole tavern fell asleep.
Enlightenment writers extolled reason as the surest guide to human progress.

cloze.text: In his speech the coach ___ the team's courage, praising every player by name.
Travel brochures ___ the virtues of the island's beaches and food but rarely mention the crowds.
She is always ___ the benefits of cold showers, though nobody else in the house is convinced.

misuse.text: The critics extolled the film as boring and badly made.
misuse.why: Extol means to praise highly, so it cannot be used for harsh criticism.

misuse.text: He extolled his anger at the referee for ten minutes.
misuse.why: You extol something good, such as a virtue or a person; anger is expressed or vented, not extolled.

synonyms.vs: Praise is everyday and can be mild; extol is formal and suggests warm, lavish, enthusiastic praise.
Laud is also formal and often public; extol often lists specific qualities or benefits.
Exalt means to raise someone to a high rank or to praise them almost as holy; extol is praise in words, often listing good points.

confusables.note: Extort means to obtain money or a promise by force or threats.

origin: From Latin extollere, 'to lift up', so to extol is to raise someone up in words.

sense: waste away through lack of use
definition: To become weaker or smaller, usually because of lack of use or lack of care.
nuance: Atrophy is used literally for muscles and organs that waste away, and figuratively for skills, institutions and feelings that fade through neglect. It is also a noun for the process. It sounds technical and slightly gloomy.

examples.text: After months in bed, his leg muscles atrophied and he had to learn to walk again.
Skills that are never practised atrophy, which is why regular review matters in language learning.
Critics warn that local democracy will atrophy if councils lose all their powers.
Without regular maintenance, the training programme will atrophy and staff skills will decline.
Over years of dull routine, his ambition had atrophied until he no longer wanted anything.
If I don't speak Spanish for a year, I'm afraid my fluency will start to atrophy.

cloze.text: Muscles that are left unused in a plaster cast begin to ___, wasting away within a few weeks.
Like a muscle that is never exercised, a skill you never practise will ___ from disuse.
A town's local newspaper, starved of readers and money, may gradually ___ through neglect and finally disappear.

misuse.text: The company atrophied rapidly, doubling in size within a year.
misuse.why: Atrophy means to waste away, so a company that doubles in size is the opposite.

misuse.text: The price of bread atrophied by ten per cent last month.
misuse.why: Atrophy is the gradual wasting of something through disuse or neglect, such as a muscle or a skill, not a fall in a price.

synonyms.vs: Wither is more literary and used for plants and hopes; atrophy is for body parts, skills and institutions.
Waste away is plain English and usually about a person or body; atrophy is more technical.

confusables.note: Hypertrophy is the opposite: growth in the size of an organ or muscle.

origin: From Greek atrophia, 'lack of nourishment'.

sense: a deep split in a group
definition: A deep split in a group or organisation, especially over a difference of belief.
nuance: Schism is used for a lasting split in a church, party or movement, usually over principles. It is stronger than a quarrel because the group actually divides. It is common in history and politics.

examples.text: The quarrel over leadership caused a schism, and the party broke into two rival groups.
The Great Schism of 1054 divided the Christian church into western and eastern branches.
There's a real schism in our family over whether to sell Grandad's house.
The committee's report warns that unless the dispute is settled, a schism within the union is likely.
The schism split the village chapel in two: half the congregation now worshipped in a barn across the road.
Historians trace the schism between the two wings of the movement to a disagreement about tactics.

cloze.text: Disagreement over doctrine grew so bitter that it led to a ___, with two churches replacing one.
In the late fourteenth century, a ___ in the Western Church left two rival popes, one in Rome and one in Avignon.
A single vote on the budget threatened to turn a quiet disagreement into a lasting ___ within the club.

misuse.text: There is a long schism in the kitchen wall where the plaster has cracked.
misuse.why: A schism is a split within a group over belief or loyalty, not a physical crack in an object.

misuse.text: The schism of the two teams ended in a happy merger.
misuse.why: A schism is a split, not a joining together, so it cannot end in a merger.

synonyms.vs: Split is everyday and works for anything; schism is formal and usually concerns beliefs or organisations.
Rift can describe a broken relationship between two people; schism is a split in a whole group.
Division is general and can be mild; schism is a serious, lasting break.

origin: From Greek schisma, 'a split', from schizein, 'to split'.

definition: A person with great knowledge and refined taste in an area such as art, food or wine.
nuance: Connoisseur describes someone who can judge fine quality and enjoys it, usually in art, wine, food or music. It is mostly approving, though it can sound a little proud. It is followed by 'of' or comes after the field: a wine connoisseur.

examples.text: My uncle is a real wine connoisseur; he can name the vineyard from one sip.
Art connoisseurs from around the world gathered in Paris for the auction of the rare painting.
Eighteenth-century connoisseurs prided themselves on telling a genuine old master from a copy.
The club's membership is open to connoisseurs and beginners alike, provided they love fine tea.
The old connoisseur held the violin up to the light and smiled: it was a genuine Stradivari.
Unlike the casual viewer, the connoisseur notices tiny differences in brushwork and colour.

cloze.text: As a cheese ___, she could tell from one taste which region and which season the cheese came from.
He is no mere beginner but a true ___ of jazz, with ten thousand records and a memory for every session.
The auction house sent its catalogue to every serious collector and ___ of antique furniture on its list.

misuse.text: He is a connoisseur of cheap fast food who eats anything without caring about taste.
misuse.why: A connoisseur has refined taste and judgement, which does not fit someone who does not care about quality.

misuse.text: The connoisseur was a famous painter who made the portrait herself.
misuse.why: A connoisseur appreciates and judges art, not creates it; the creator is an artist.

synonyms.vs: Expert may have skills or professional knowledge; connoisseur stresses refined taste and appreciation.
Aficionado means an enthusiastic fan; connoisseur stresses fine judgement over passion.
Buff is informal and means a keen enthusiast, as in a film buff.

origin: From an older French spelling of connaisseur, 'one who knows', from connaître, 'to know'.

sense: argue that a claim is false
definition: To argue that a claim or accusation is false, usually by giving evidence.
nuance: Rebut is used in debate, law and academic writing when someone answers a charge or argument point by point. It describes the attempt, whether or not it succeeds. The object is a claim, an accusation or an argument.

examples.text: The company issued a statement to rebut the claims, saying the figures were wrong.
Smith's reply seeks to rebut each of the objections raised by his critics.
He tried to rebut my point with a single weak example.
The defence called an expert to rebut the evidence presented by the prosecution.
She opened her mouth to rebut the accusation, but no words came.
A good essay anticipates counterarguments and rebuts them in turn.

cloze.text: After the newspaper accused her of lying, the minister published the documents to ___ the story.
In the debate, each speaker had two minutes to ___ the other side's points, answering them one by one with evidence.
Lawyers for the company will try to ___ the charges by showing that the accounts were correct.

misuse.text: He rebutted the invitation politely and stayed at home.
misuse.why: You rebut a claim or argument; for declining an invitation use 'decline' or 'turn down'.

misuse.text: My teacher rebutted me for talking in class.
misuse.why: Rebut means to argue that a claim is false; telling someone off is 'rebuke'.

phrases: In order to rebut this objection,...

synonyms.vs: Refute claims to have proved something false; rebut only means to argue against it, whether or not it succeeds.
Counter is shorter and more general; rebut specifically answers a claim with evidence or argument.
Contradict says the opposite is true; rebut also gives reasons or evidence.

confusables.note: Rebuff means to reject someone or something sharply, such as an offer, not to argue against a claim.
Rebuke means to tell someone off sharply for something they did.

definition: To describe or mark out something precisely, showing its exact outline, limits or details.
nuance: Delineate is used for drawing clear lines, whether on a map or in an argument. In essays it often means setting out the scope or boundaries of a topic. The object is usually a border, role, duty or concept.

examples.text: The map delineates the border between the two countries, showing exactly where each one begins and ends.
The first chapter delineates the scope of the study and explains which questions it will not address.
Can you delineate what each of us is responsible for before we start?
New guidelines delineate which jobs may be done from home and which must be done in the office.
The streetlamp delineated her face against the dark window, every line sharp and clear.
Researchers must clearly delineate the groups being compared, or the results will be hard to interpret.

cloze.text: The contract must ___ each party's duties clearly, so that nobody can later claim confusion.
In the introduction, the author tries to ___ the limits of the topic and say which questions are left aside.
A thick white line ___ the boundary of the property, marking out its exact edge from the road to the river.

misuse.text: She delineated the whole report by deleting it from the computer.
misuse.why: Delineate means to describe or mark out clearly, not to remove or destroy.

misuse.text: The first chapter delineates about the main risks of the project.
misuse.why: Delineate takes a direct object: the chapter delineates the main risks, not 'about' them.

synonyms.vs: Outline gives only the main points; delineate stresses precision about edges and limits.
Define gives the exact meaning of a term; delineate often marks the boundaries of an area or role.
Demarcate is closer to marking a border between areas; delineate can also describe in words.

origin: From Latin delineare, 'to sketch out', from linea, 'line'.

sense: believing in equal rights and status
definition: Believing that everyone should have the same rights, status and chances in life.
nuance: Egalitarian describes people, societies, rules and organisations built on fairness between all members. It is mostly approving, though critics sometimes call egalitarian ideals unrealistic. It is common in politics, sociology and anthropology.

examples.text: Our office is very egalitarian: the director sits at an ordinary desk and eats in the same canteen as everyone else.
Anthropologists describe many hunter-gatherer societies as egalitarian, since food was shared and nobody ruled.
The party promises a more egalitarian tax system in which the richest pay a larger share.
The school's egalitarian ethos means that every pupil, whatever their background, receives the same opportunities.
In the new colony, they dreamed of an egalitarian life with no masters and no servants.
Critics doubt that a truly egalitarian society can survive without some form of leadership.

cloze.text: In an ___ community, nobody is born into a higher rank and every adult has the same vote.
The founders wanted an ___ college, open to rich and poor students alike and with special privileges for no one.
She prefers a flat, ___ company structure, in which every employee has the same say whatever their job title.

misuse.text: The egalitarian king gave all the power to himself and his family.
misuse.why: Egalitarian means believing in equal rights, so concentrating all power in one family is the opposite.

misuse.text: Mum cut the cake into egalitarian slices so that everyone got the same amount.
misuse.why: Egalitarian describes beliefs and societies built on equal rights, not things that are simply the same size; say 'equal slices'.

synonyms.vs: Classless means with no social classes at all; egalitarian is a belief or principle that may be only partly achieved.
Democratic suggests rule by the people or shared decision-making; egalitarian is about equal status and rewards.
Fair is everyday and general; egalitarian is a formal, political word about equal rights.

confusables.note: Equitable means fair and reasonable, not necessarily equal.

origin: From French égalitaire, from égal, 'equal'.

definition: To join or combine several things, groups or companies into one.
nuance: Amalgamate is used for organisations, companies, schools and ideas that merge into a single whole. It is common in business, administration and academic writing. It can be used with or without an object: two firms amalgamate, or a manager amalgamates them.

examples.text: The two small banks agreed to amalgamate, forming a single company with over a thousand branches.
Over centuries, local dialects amalgamated into a single national language.
We should amalgamate these three spreadsheets instead of juggling them all.
The council voted to amalgamate the two primary schools to save money.
In his strange paintings, the faces of strangers amalgamated into one haunting figure.
The author amalgamates ideas from sociology, history and economics into a single theory.

cloze.text: To cut costs, the university plans to ___ its three small departments into one large school.
Over the years the villages slowly ___, until they were one town with a single council.
The report ___ data from five separate surveys into a single table, so readers see one clear picture.

misuse.text: The new manager amalgamated the department into three separate teams.
misuse.why: Amalgamate means to join things into one; splitting one department into three is the opposite.

misuse.text: The two clubs amalgamated each other last year.
misuse.why: Without an object, amalgamate needs no 'each other': the two clubs amalgamated, or one amalgamated with the other.

synonyms.vs: Merge is everyday and general; amalgamate sounds more formal and suggests different things blending into one whole.
Combine is the plain word for joining; amalgamate usually describes organisations or ideas that become one.
Consolidate means to join and strengthen, often to save money; amalgamate focuses on becoming one.

definition: From this moment onwards; starting now and continuing in the future.
nuance: Henceforth is a formal, slightly old-fashioned adverb used in rules, announcements, contracts and academic definitions. It looks forward from the moment of speaking or writing. It often starts a sentence or comes before a verb phrase.

examples.text: Henceforth, all staff must sign in at the front desk before entering the building.
The prime minister announced that henceforth no new licences would be granted.
Henceforth, I shall be waking up at six and going for a run. Wish me luck.
The term is used here in its narrow sense and will henceforth refer only to written texts.
'Henceforth you will be known as Sir Edmund,' said the king, touching the sword to his shoulder.
The two clubs have merged and will henceforth play under a single name and in new colours.

cloze.text: The old rules are cancelled; ___, every request must go through the new online form.
She promised that ___ she would tell the truth, even when it was uncomfortable.
In this essay I use 'the state' to mean the national government, and ___ the term will always carry that meaning.

misuse.text: Henceforth I was born in a small village near the sea.
misuse.why: Henceforth points forward from now, so it cannot describe a past event like a birth.

misuse.text: The sample was very small; henceforth, the results cannot be trusted.
misuse.why: Henceforth means from now on, not 'therefore'; to give a consequence, use 'hence' or 'thus'.

synonyms.vs: From now on is everyday and spoken; henceforth is formal and common in rules and announcements.
Hereafter is similar but more legal, and can also mean after death.

confusables.note: Thenceforth means from that time on, looking back at a past moment, not from now.
Hence usually means 'for this reason'; henceforth only means 'from now on'.

definition: Anger caused by something that seems unfair, insulting or wrong.
nuance: Indignation is anger with a moral side: you feel it when something seems unjust or disrespectful. It is common in news, history and literature, often as 'public indignation' or 'righteous indignation'. It is a stronger and more principled feeling than simple annoyance.

examples.text: The decision to close the library provoked widespread indignation among local families.
I was full of indignation when they charged me again for a bag I'd already paid for.
Historians note that public indignation at the tax, rather than its cost, drove the protests.
The committee expressed its indignation at the way the staff had been treated.
'How dare you!' he cried, red in the face with indignation.
Moral indignation can motivate reform, but it can also blind people to the facts.

cloze.text: The unfair ban on the team's captain caused such ___ among fans that thousands signed a petition.
She spoke with ___ about the shopkeeper who had accused her of stealing when she had paid in full.
His face flushed with righteous ___ when he realised he had been left out of the meeting on purpose.

misuse.text: She felt great indignation when she won the lottery.
misuse.why: Indignation is anger at something unfair; winning the lottery calls for delight, not indignation.

misuse.text: She sighed with indignation, tired after a long day, and went to bed.
misuse.why: Indignation is anger at an injustice, not tiredness or boredom.

synonyms.vs: Outrage is stronger and often public and loud; indignation is anger at unfairness, sometimes more restrained.
Resentment is a long-lasting bitter feeling; indignation is a sharp reaction to a particular wrong.
Fury is intense and uncontrolled anger of any kind; indignation always involves a sense of injustice.

confusables.note: An indignity is an insult or humiliating treatment, not the anger itself.
Indigence is a formal word for poverty.

origin: From Latin indignatio, from indignari, 'to regard as unworthy'.

definition: Just beginning to exist or develop, and not yet fully formed.
nuance: Nascent describes new industries, movements, ideas and feelings that are only starting to appear. It suggests potential and is neutral or hopeful in tone. It is common in business, history and science writing.

examples.text: The nascent industry, only two years old, already employs five hundred people.
Historians trace the nascent labour movement to the factory towns of the early nineteenth century.
It's still a nascent idea, so please don't judge it too harshly yet.
The ministry will fund nascent technologies that are not yet ready for commercial use.
She felt a nascent hope, small and fragile, that things might be all right.
The nascent field of genetics had few methods, but its questions were bold.

cloze.text: The company is still ___, with only three employees and a first product not yet launched.
Investors tend to avoid ___ markets, where nobody yet knows whether customers will appear.
A ___ friendship was starting to grow between the two girls, though they had met only twice.

misuse.text: The nascent empire collapsed after eight hundred years.
misuse.why: Nascent means just beginning, so an empire that lasted eight centuries was not nascent at its end.

misuse.text: Smartphones are a nascent technology that almost everyone has used for over a decade.
misuse.why: Nascent means only just beginning; a technology in everyday use for years is established, not nascent.

synonyms.vs: Emerging is plain and common; nascent is more formal and stresses that something is only just starting.
Budding is warmer, often about a person's talent; nascent is used for movements, industries and ideas.
Embryonic suggests an early stage with full growth still to come; nascent can also describe small signs of something new.

confusables.note: Natal means relating to birth.

origin: From Latin nascens, 'being born', from nasci, 'to be born'.

definition: Careful good sense in avoiding risks and planning for the future.
nuance: Prudence is a quality of judgement: thinking ahead, avoiding unnecessary risk and managing resources wisely. It is approving, but can sound cautious or dull. It is common in finance, ethics and political writing.

examples.text: Showing great prudence, she saved a third of her wages every month in case of emergencies.
Economists praised the minister's prudence in building up reserves before the downturn.
Call it prudence, but I always keep some cash at home in case the cards stop working.
Aristotle treats prudence as the virtue that lets a person choose well in practical situations.
The regulator urged banks to act with prudence when lending to risky borrowers.
Prudence, rather than courage, guided the general's decision to wait for reinforcements.

cloze.text: The chancellor promised fiscal ___: no extra borrowing and no spending that the country could not afford.
Her ___ with money, saving carefully and avoiding debt, left her comfortable in old age.
Some call it cowardice, but he called it ___: waiting for better weather before climbing the mountain.

misuse.text: He bought a sports car on impulse, a clear act of prudence.
misuse.why: Prudence means careful good sense, so an impulse purchase is the opposite.

misuse.text: Her prudence about kissing scenes made her walk out of the film.
misuse.why: Being easily shocked by sexual matters is prudishness or prudery; prudence is careful good sense about risk.

synonyms.vs: Caution focuses on avoiding danger; prudence also includes planning ahead and good judgement.
Discretion is about tact and keeping quiet; prudence is about avoiding risk.
Thrift is about saving and not wasting money; prudence is wider, covering any careful planning.

confusables.note: Prudery means being easily shocked by anything to do with sex.

origin: From Latin prudentia, a shortened form of providentia, 'foresight'.

definition: Difficult to control or keep in order, especially noisy, wild or disobedient.
nuance: Unruly describes children, crowds, animals and even hair that will not stay under control. It is common in news about disorder and in everyday talk about behaviour. It suggests a lack of discipline rather than deliberate cruelty.

examples.text: The unruly children ran around the restaurant, ignoring every request to sit down.
Police were called to deal with unruly fans who had thrown bottles onto the pitch.
Studies of classroom behaviour show that unruly pupils often respond best to clear, consistent rules.
Passengers who become unruly on the aircraft may be fined or banned from future flights.
She tried to tame her unruly hair with a comb, but the curls sprang back at once.
Medieval rulers feared the unruly crowd as a danger to order.

cloze.text: The teacher found it hard to calm the ___ class, which shouted and threw paper across the room.
No comb or brush could control her ___ curls, which stood up wildly in every direction.
Airlines may refuse to carry passengers who have been loud, drunk and ___ on earlier flights.

misuse.text: The unruly student sat quietly and obeyed every rule.
misuse.why: Unruly means hard to control, so a quiet student who obeys every rule is the opposite.

misuse.text: The children behaved unruly all through the party.
misuse.why: Unruly is an adjective, not an adverb: say the children were unruly, or behaved badly.

synonyms.vs: Disorderly is formal and often legal, as in 'disorderly conduct'; unruly is more general and often about children or crowds.
Rowdy means noisy and rough, often in fun; unruly adds refusing to be controlled.
Disobedient is about ignoring a particular order; unruly describes a general lack of control.

confusables.note: Unruffled means calm and not upset.

origin: Formed from un-, 'not', and the old word ruly, 'obedient to rules'.

definition: Extremely bad; of a very poor standard.
nuance: Abysmal is a strong word of criticism for performance, conditions or results that are far below any acceptable standard. It is common in news, reviews and everyday complaints. It is stronger than 'poor' or 'bad'.

examples.text: The food was abysmal: cold, tasteless and served an hour late.
The government's record on housing has been described as abysmal by its own advisers.
Literacy rates in the region were abysmal in 1900, with fewer than one in ten adults able to read.
The inspectors rated the school's safety standards as abysmal and demanded immediate action.
His handwriting was abysmal, a tangle of loops that no one could read.
After an abysmal first half, the team scored three goals and won the match.

cloze.text: The hotel's service was ___: nobody answered the phone, the room was dirty and the bill was wrong.
She was ashamed of her ___ exam results; she had failed every single paper.
Conditions in the old hospital were ___, with leaking roofs, no heating and too few nurses.

misuse.text: The abysmal view from the top of the mountain took our breath away.
misuse.why: Abysmal means extremely bad, so it cannot describe a stunning view; use 'breathtaking' or 'magnificent'.

misuse.text: Her abysmal performance won her first prize.
misuse.why: Abysmal means very bad, so it does not fit a winning performance.

synonyms.vs: Appalling suggests shock and horror at something bad; abysmal stresses a very low standard.
Dreadful is everyday and general; abysmal is stronger and common with results or performance.
Atrocious can also describe cruel, shocking acts, as in atrocious crimes; abysmal is only about a very low standard.

confusables.note: Abyssal means relating to the deepest parts of the ocean.

origin: From abyss, from Greek abyssos, 'bottomless'.

definition: Done quickly, without attention to detail, so not thorough.
nuance: Cursory describes glances, checks, readings and inspections that are too fast to be reliable. It is mildly critical and common in reports and essay feedback. It is usually followed by a noun such as 'glance' or 'examination'.

examples.text: The guard gave my ticket a cursory glance and waved me through without really looking.
A cursory reading of the text suggests agreement, but a careful one reveals a sharp disagreement.
Inspectors made only a cursory check of the building before approving it.
The committee's cursory review of the application failed to notice the missing documents.
He gave the room a cursory look and, seeing nobody, hurried on.
Cursory treatment of the evidence weakens an otherwise lively argument.

cloze.text: The police made only a ___ search of the flat, glancing in the cupboards and leaving within minutes.
A ___ reading of the contract is not enough; you must study every clause and footnote.
The doctor's ___ examination, lasting barely two minutes, missed the real cause of the pain.

misuse.text: She gave the problem cursory attention, studying it carefully for several weeks.
misuse.why: Cursory means quick and shallow, so careful study over weeks is the opposite.

misuse.text: The cursory inspection found every tiny fault in the engine.
misuse.why: A cursory inspection is too hasty to find every tiny fault; that would need a thorough one.

synonyms.vs: Perfunctory suggests doing something only as a duty, with no real interest; cursory stresses speed and lack of detail.
Superficial means lacking depth of understanding; cursory describes a quick act.
Hasty is about hurry, often with poor results; cursory is about a brief look that skips details.

confusables.note: Cursive is joined-up handwriting.

origin: From Latin cursorius, 'of a runner', from currere, 'to run': a cursory look just runs over the surface.

definition: A serious lack or shortage of something that is needed.
nuance: Dearth is used for a shortage that is striking or harmful, usually with 'of'. It is common in news, reports and academic writing about resources, evidence and talent. It sounds more formal than 'shortage' or 'lack'.

examples.text: A dearth of affordable homes is forcing young people to leave the city.
The study notes a dearth of reliable data on the early years of the industry.
There's a dearth of good coffee shops round here; I have to walk twenty minutes.
The department reported a dearth of qualified applicants for senior posts.
In the village there was a dearth of laughter that winter, as the harvest had failed.
Researchers lament the dearth of women in the early scientific records.

cloze.text: Because of a ___ of nurses, patients wait hours to be seen even for minor injuries.
There is certainly no ___ of volunteers; more than two hundred people applied for ten places.
The historians complained of a ___ of written sources, which made the period hard to study.

misuse.text: The farmer had a dearth of apples, enough to fill ten lorries.
misuse.why: Dearth means a serious lack, so having enough apples to fill ten lorries is the opposite.

misuse.text: A dearth of snow covered the roads, and traffic stopped.
misuse.why: A dearth is a lack of something, so it cannot be a heavy fall that covers roads.

synonyms.vs: Shortage is everyday and usually practical; dearth is formal and suggests a striking lack.
Scarcity is a general state of being hard to find; dearth is a particular lack of something needed.
Paucity is even more formal and literary, meaning a very small amount.

confusables.note: Death is the end of life; dearth is an unrelated word.

origin: From Middle English derthe, from dere, 'dear' in the old sense of costly, since scarce food was expensive.

definition: Wishing to cause harm or suffering to others; full of ill will.
nuance: Malevolent describes people, looks, intentions and forces that seem to want to hurt or destroy. It is strongly negative and common in fiction, literary criticism and descriptions of crime. It is about wishing evil, not just being unkind by accident.

examples.text: The malevolent stepmother watched the girl closely, hoping she would fail and be sent away.
The play presents Iago as a malevolent schemer who destroys others simply for pleasure.
The cat gave me a malevolent stare, as if it were planning revenge for the bath.
The judge described the attack as a malevolent act intended to cause maximum suffering.
The report found no evidence of malevolent intent; the errors were due to carelessness.
Folk tales often cast malevolent spirits as the cause of illness and bad luck.

cloze.text: The villain's ___ smile showed that he enjoyed other people's pain.
Far from being benevolent, the old king was openly ___, delighting in the suffering of his subjects.
In the old story, a ___ witch cursed the village, hoping to bring suffering to every family.

misuse.text: The malevolent nurse cared kindly for every patient.
misuse.why: Malevolent means wishing harm, so it clashes with kind care.

misuse.text: He gave a malevolent speech full of good wishes for the newlyweds.
misuse.why: A malevolent speech would express ill will, not good wishes.

synonyms.vs: Malicious is more common and often about actions meant to hurt; malevolent describes a deeper, lasting wish for harm.
Spiteful is smaller and petty; malevolent suggests serious, threatening ill will.
Malign can mean harmful in effect; malevolent stresses the ill will behind it.

confusables.note: Malignant is used of diseases such as cancer, or of a very harmful influence.

origin: From Latin malevolens, 'wishing evil', from male, 'badly', and volens, 'wishing'.

sense: remarkably great in size or amount
definition: Remarkably large, great or impressive in amount, size or ability.
nuance: Prodigious is used for amounts, efforts and talents so great that they cause wonder. It is approving or awed. It is common with words like talent, memory, appetite, effort and output.

examples.text: The young pianist showed prodigious talent, performing difficult concertos from memory at the age of ten.
Darwin collected a prodigious quantity of specimens during the voyage.
My little brother has a prodigious appetite; he finished three burgers and asked for more.
The project demanded a prodigious amount of effort from a very small team.
A prodigious wave rose over the harbour wall and swallowed the fishing boats.
Her prodigious memory allowed the scholar to quote whole chapters from texts she had read decades earlier.

cloze.text: The author's ___ output, over eighty novels in thirty years, astonished even his publisher.
Building the cathedral required a ___ amount of stone, labour and time, far beyond what anyone expected.
At seven, the girl already showed ___ talent, composing music that adults found hard to believe.

misuse.text: After years of wasting money abroad, the prodigious son came home to ask his father's forgiveness.
misuse.why: The wasteful son of the story is 'prodigal'; prodigious means remarkably great in size, amount or ability.

misuse.text: He made a prodigious effort, but it was small and barely noticeable.
misuse.why: A prodigious effort is enormous and remarkable, so it cannot be small and barely noticeable.

synonyms.vs: Immense is plain and about size; prodigious adds a sense of wonder at the amount or skill.
Phenomenal is informal and enthusiastic; prodigious is more formal and often about amounts or abilities.
Colossal stresses huge physical size; prodigious is wider and often describes talent or effort.

confusables.note: Prodigal means wastefully extravagant with money.

origin: From Latin prodigium, 'an omen' or 'a marvel'.

sense: act as judge in a dispute
definition: To act as judge in a dispute or competition and give an official decision.
nuance: Adjudicate is used for courts, panels, tribunals and judges who hear both sides and decide. It suggests a neutral, official role. It is common in law, politics and competitions, with 'between' or a noun like 'dispute' or 'claim'.

examples.text: A retired judge was appointed to adjudicate the dispute, hearing both sides before announcing who was right.
Under the contract, any disagreement will be adjudicated by a neutral third party.
Mum had to adjudicate whenever my brother and I argued over the remote.
Courts must adjudicate between competing rights when two freedoms conflict.
The village elder adjudicated the quarrel over the boundary stone, and neither farmer dared to argue.
Scholars cannot adjudicate the question without further evidence from the archives.

cloze.text: The tribunal will ___ claims of unfair dismissal and decide whether the workers are owed compensation.
Three experts were chosen to ___ the poetry competition and announce the winner.
When neighbours cannot agree about a fence, the local court can ___ and give a binding ruling.

misuse.text: The judge adjudicated the trial until Monday because a key witness was ill.
misuse.why: To pause a trial until later is to adjourn it; adjudicate means to hear a dispute and decide it.

misuse.text: She adjudicated the argument by joining one side and shouting the loudest.
misuse.why: Adjudicate needs a neutral, official decision; taking a side is not adjudicating.

synonyms.vs: Judge is everyday and general; adjudicate is formal and suggests an official decision in a dispute.
Arbitrate suggests both sides agreed to accept an outsider's decision; adjudicate can be imposed by a court.
Rule on is plainer and common in law; adjudicate stresses the whole process of hearing and deciding.

confusables.note: Adjourn means to pause or end a meeting or court session until later.

origin: From Latin adjudicare, 'to award judicially'.

definition: To increase rapidly in number or spread quickly, often more than is wanted.
nuance: Proliferate is used for things that multiply fast: shops, rumours, weapons, bacteria, regulations. It often suggests growth that is hard to control, though it can be neutral. It is common in news and science.

examples.text: Fast-food outlets have proliferated along the high street, doubling in number in five years.
Bacteria proliferate quickly in warm, damp conditions, which is why food must be kept cool.
Coffee shops seem to proliferate in this city; there's a new one every month.
Regulators warn that fake websites are proliferating faster than they can be shut down.
Rumours proliferated through the camp, each wilder than the last.
After the invention of printing, pamphlets and newspapers proliferated across Europe.

cloze.text: Without strict rules, cheap imitations of the product will ___ and flood the market.
In warm weather, weeds ___ across the garden so quickly that it is hard to keep up.
Since the law changed, betting shops have ___ on the high street: there were two in 2010 and there are fifteen now.

misuse.text: The number of wild tigers has proliferated; only a few hundred remain.
misuse.why: Proliferate means to increase rapidly, so it does not fit a species that is nearly gone.

misuse.text: The government plans to proliferate the use of electric cars.
misuse.why: Proliferate usually has no object: things proliferate by themselves. To make something more common, say 'promote' or 'encourage'.

synonyms.vs: Multiply is everyday and neutral; proliferate is formal and often suggests uncontrolled growth.
Spread is general; proliferate stresses growth in number.
Mushroom is informal and vivid; proliferate is the formal equivalent.

confusables.note: Profligate means wasteful with money.

sense: extend known facts to unknown cases
definition: To use known facts or trends to work out what is probably true elsewhere or in the future.
nuance: Extrapolate is a key word in science, economics and argument when you extend a pattern beyond the data you have. It often carries a warning: extrapolating can be risky if the pattern does not continue. It is usually followed by 'from'.

examples.text: Scientists extrapolated from last year's figures to predict how many people would catch the disease next winter.
It is risky to extrapolate from a sample of forty people to the whole population.
You can't extrapolate from one bad meal that the whole restaurant is awful.
Analysts extrapolate future demand from current sales, assuming that growth continues at the same rate.
Watching the floodwater climb one step every hour, she extrapolated grimly: by midnight it would reach the bedrooms.
Extrapolating beyond the range of the data assumes that the pattern continues, which may not be true.

cloze.text: It is unwise to ___ from a tiny sample to the whole country, because the pattern may not hold.
Economists ___ next year's growth from the past five years, assuming the trend simply continues.
If you ___ the current trend, the city's population will double by 2060, though few planners expect that to happen.

misuse.text: The researcher extrapolated the key quotations from the interviews and put them in a table.
misuse.why: Taking quotations out is extracting them; extrapolate means extending a trend or pattern to cases beyond the data.

misuse.text: He extrapolated the data by deleting half of it.
misuse.why: Extrapolate means to extend a pattern beyond the data you have; deleting data is not extrapolating.

phrases: ...we can extrapolate from these findings that...

synonyms.vs: Infer draws a conclusion from evidence of any kind; extrapolate extends a known pattern beyond the observed range.
Project is similar for forecasting numbers; extrapolate stresses extending an observed pattern.
Generalise applies a finding to a wider group; extrapolate also extends to the future or unseen cases.

confusables.note: Interpolate means to estimate a value between known points, or to insert something into a text.

definition: A person who is famous and greatly respected in a particular field.
nuance: Luminary describes someone eminent in their field, such as science, art, law or sport. It is approving and a little grand, often used in the plural for a gathering of notable people. It is common in news and cultural writing.

examples.text: Leading luminaries of the film world, including three Oscar winners, attended the opening.
Newton and other scientific luminaries of the seventeenth century corresponded across Europe.
My professor is a luminary in her field; people fly in to hear her speak.
The conference will feature talks by luminaries from law, medicine and engineering.
Among the luminaries at the dinner sat an old poet whom everyone treated with reverence.
Few literary luminaries of the period came from working-class backgrounds.

cloze.text: At the gala, the city's artistic ___ gathered to honour the painter who had made it famous.
She became a ___ of the legal world, quoted by judges and consulted by presidents.
Scientific ___ from three continents joined the panel, each one famous for a major discovery.

misuse.text: The watch has a luminary face that glows in the dark.
misuse.why: Something that glows is luminous; a luminary is a famous, respected person, and the word is a noun.

misuse.text: The luminary was ignored by everyone and quite unknown.
misuse.why: A luminary is well known and respected, so being unknown is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Celebrity is about fame; luminary is about respect and achievement in a field.
Notable is plainer and can describe any noteworthy person; luminary is warmer and grander.
Star is informal and often about popularity; luminary suggests lasting respect.

confusables.note: Luminous means giving off light.

origin: From Latin luminare, 'a source of light', from lumen, 'light'.

definition: To take the place of something or someone, usually because you are newer or better.
nuance: Supplant means to replace something established, often by pushing it aside. It is used for technologies, theories and rivals, and it can suggest force or ambition. It is common in history, business and politics.

examples.text: Email has largely supplanted the fax machine in offices across the country.
Steam power gradually supplanted water power as factories moved to the cities.
Streaming has supplanted DVDs; I don't know anyone who still buys them.
The new regulations supplant all earlier guidelines on safety in the workplace.
He feared that the new apprentice would supplant him as the master's favourite.
Critics argued that the theory failed to supplant older explanations because it explained less.

cloze.text: Electric cars may eventually ___ petrol engines, which would then be seen only in museums.
The young minister plotted to ___ the prime minister and take over the party leadership.
Online banking has begun to ___ visits to the bank, which many branches now find almost empty.

misuse.text: The new tools supplanted the old ones, so now we use both.
misuse.why: Supplant means to take the place of, so the old tools would no longer be used.

misuse.text: She supplanted her diet with iron tablets to make sure she got enough.
misuse.why: Adding something extra is to supplement it; supplant would mean the tablets replaced her food entirely.

synonyms.vs: Replace is general and neutral; supplant suggests the new thing pushed out the old, often by force or merit.
Supersede is formal for something becoming out of date because a newer thing takes its place; supplant can suggest rivalry.
Oust means to force someone out of a position; supplant also means taking their place.

confusables.note: Supplement means to add to something, not to replace it.

origin: From Latin supplantare, 'to trip up', from planta, 'sole of the foot'.

sense: unfairness in how people are treated
definition: Unfairness in the way people are treated or in how resources are shared.
nuance: Inequity is used in policy, economics and ethics for unfair differences in treatment or distribution, as in health, education or pay. It is more critical than 'inequality' because it says the difference is unjust. It is common in reports and essays.

examples.text: Campaigners say the funding system creates inequity, giving rich schools far more money than poor ones.
Health inequity persists because poorer neighbourhoods have fewer clinics and less access to fresh food.
It's a real inequity that she does the same job but gets paid less.
The commission was set up to examine historic inequities in land ownership.
He had grown up watching the inequity between the grand manor and the cottages below.
Scholars distinguish inequity, a judgement about fairness, from simple inequality, a measurable difference.

cloze.text: Paying women less than men for identical work is a clear ___ that the law must correct.
Public health experts call an avoidable, unjust gap in health between rich and poor a health ___, not merely a difference.
Reformers hoped to remove the ___ in the tax system, where wage earners paid more than landowners.

misuse.text: Her inequity was that she was too generous with her friends.
misuse.why: Inequity means unfairness in treatment or distribution; generosity is not an inequity.

misuse.text: The inequity between the twins' heights was one centimetre.
misuse.why: Inequity is an unfair difference, not simply a measurable one like height.

synonyms.vs: Unfairness is the everyday word; inequity is formal and common in policy and research.
Injustice is stronger and often about breaking rights or laws; inequity is about unfair distribution.
Inequality is a measurable difference that may or may not be unfair; inequity says the difference is unfair.

confusables.note: Iniquity means wickedness or serious sin.

sense: steal money you were trusted with
definition: To steal money that you have been trusted to look after, especially from an employer.
nuance: Embezzle is a legal and news word for theft by someone who has legitimate access to money, such as a treasurer or accountant. It is stronger than 'misuse'. The object is money, funds or property entrusted to the thief.

examples.text: The treasurer was jailed for embezzling thousands of pounds from the village charity.
Employees who embezzle company funds face dismissal and criminal charges.
Apparently the accountant had been embezzling money for years before anyone noticed.
Historians record that the governor embezzled public funds meant for building roads.
She discovered that her uncle had embezzled the family savings to pay his gambling debts.
Auditing systems exist partly to make it harder to embezzle money without being detected.

cloze.text: The cashier was caught trying to ___ small sums from the till over many months.
He used his position as treasurer to ___ money from the club, then covered it up with false accounts.
Investigators found that the manager had ___ millions from the pension fund entrusted to his care.

misuse.text: A burglar embezzled the shop at night.
misuse.why: Embezzle means stealing money you were trusted to manage; a burglar breaks in and steals, which is not embezzlement.

misuse.text: She embezzled her own savings and spent them on a holiday.
misuse.why: You cannot embezzle your own money; it must belong to someone else who trusted you.

synonyms.vs: Misappropriate is more formal and can include misusing funds without outright theft.
Steal is general; embezzle needs a position of trust over the money.
Defraud means to cheat someone out of money or rights by deceit; embezzle is stealing what you manage.

definition: A standard or example by which other things are judged.
nuance: Touchstone is used for a model, test or reference point that reveals real quality. It is common in criticism, history and essays about values. It is approving: something that is a touchstone is trusted.

examples.text: For decades, the novel served as a touchstone against which other war writing was measured.
Her speech became the touchstone for how politicians should address the crisis.
My touchstone for a good curry is whether it tastes like my grandmother's.
The committee uses the charter as its touchstone when assessing every new proposal.
To the young poet, the old master's verse was the touchstone of all true writing.
Fairness is the touchstone of any legal system worth the name.

cloze.text: The 1966 final remains the ___ by which every later World Cup is judged.
Just as goldsmiths once rubbed metal on a dark stone to test its purity, critics use this novel as a ___ for judging new crime fiction.
For many critics, her debut album became the ___ against which they measured all her later work.

misuse.text: The mayor laid the touchstone of the new library at a public ceremony.
misuse.why: The first stone laid at a ceremony is the foundation stone; a touchstone is a standard for judging quality.

misuse.text: He bought a touchstone for his phone so it could respond to taps.
misuse.why: Touchstone is a reference point for judging quality; it is not a touchscreen.

synonyms.vs: Benchmark is a measurable standard; touchstone is a reference point of quality, often an example or principle.
Yardstick is plain and mostly about measuring; touchstone is more literary and about quality.
Criterion is a formal rule for judging; touchstone is an example or test that reveals real quality.

confusables.note: A keystone is the central stone of an arch, or the central idea that holds everything together.

origin: Originally a dark stone on which gold or silver was rubbed to test how pure it was.

definition: To make someone very annoyed and impatient, usually because of something repeated or unhelpful.
nuance: Exasperate describes a wearying, impatient kind of annoyance, often at repeated behaviour or delay. The object is a person, never a problem. Do not confuse it with 'exacerbate', which means to make something worse.

examples.text: The toddler's constant questions exasperated her mother, who had already answered each one twice.
Residents say the council's delays have exasperated even its supporters.
It exasperated him that she never listened and always did the opposite.
The tribunal noted that the repeated requests for the same documents had exasperated the applicant.
Studies of customer service show that being transferred between departments exasperates callers more than a long wait.
Exasperating delays in the peace talks left diplomats close to giving up.

cloze.text: It ___ the teacher that the class kept asking the same question after she had answered it.
Her brother's habit of leaving dirty plates everywhere never fails to ___ her.
Stop ___ me with your excuses; I've heard them all before and I am nearly out of patience.

misuse.text: The cold weather exasperated the ice on the lake, making it thicker.
misuse.why: Exasperate is about annoying a person; for making a situation worse use exacerbate.

misuse.text: She was exasperated with joy when she won the race.
misuse.why: Exasperate means to annoy greatly, so it does not fit joy.

synonyms.vs: Irritate is milder; exasperate is a stronger, wearier annoyance.
Infuriate means to make furious; exasperate stresses weary impatience.
Annoy is the everyday word; exasperate is more formal and stronger.

confusables.note: Exacerbate means to make a problem worse; exasperate means to annoy someone greatly.

origin: From Latin exasperare, 'to roughen, irritate', from asper, 'rough'.

definition: A feeling of annoyed disappointment or embarrassment after a failure or mistake.
nuance: Chagrin is a mix of annoyance, embarrassment and disappointment when things go wrong, especially when it is your own fault or a surprise. It is often used in the phrase 'to my chagrin' or 'much to his chagrin'. It sounds formal and a little literary.

examples.text: To my chagrin, I realised I had been talking about the wrong book for ten minutes.
Much to the coach's chagrin, his best player was injured in the first minute.
Much to the author's chagrin, reviewers praised the minor chapters and ignored his central argument.
The minister admitted with some chagrin that the figures had been wrong.
He watched with chagrin as his rival collected the prize he had worked so hard to win.
The student's chagrin was clear when her thesis was returned covered in corrections.

cloze.text: To his great ___, he discovered after the party that he had spinach in his teeth all evening.
She hid her ___ at losing the election and smiled as she congratulated the winner.
Much to the team's ___, the match they were sure of winning ended in a humiliating defeat.

misuse.text: She smiled with chagrin when she heard the wonderful news.
misuse.why: Chagrin is annoyed disappointment, so it does not go with wonderful news.

misuse.text: She was very chagrin when she missed the last train home.
misuse.why: Chagrin is a noun; say 'much to her chagrin' or use the adjective 'chagrined'.

synonyms.vs: Mortification is deeper embarrassment, close to shame; chagrin is annoyed disappointment.
Dismay is alarm at bad news; chagrin is the annoyance of a failure that touches your pride.
Annoyance is mild and everyday; chagrin is more formal and includes embarrassment.

definition: To annoy someone slightly, especially in a persistent way.
nuance: Irk is a short, slightly formal verb for minor but nagging annoyance. It is common in journalism and fiction, often as 'it irks me that' or 'irked by'. It is milder than 'infuriate'.

examples.text: It really irks me when people talk loudly on the phone on the train.
The new parking charges have irked local shop owners, who say customers will stay away.
Her careless humming irked him all through the long afternoon.
Minor delays at the border irked travellers but caused no serious harm.
Students are often irked by assignments that seem to have no clear purpose.
What irked the critics was not the film's violence but its refusal to explain it.

cloze.text: His habit of tapping the table during meetings began to ___ everyone on the team.
It ___ her that her brother never said thank you, even after she had cooked all day.
Small things, such as a dripping tap or an unanswered text, can ___ us more than big problems.

misuse.text: The earthquake irked the whole city and killed thousands.
misuse.why: Irk means mild annoyance, far too weak for a disaster that kills people.

misuse.text: I am irking about the noise from next door.
misuse.why: Irk needs the annoyed person as its object: the noise irks me, or I am irked by it.

synonyms.vs: Annoy is the everyday word; irk is slightly more formal and often milder and longer-lasting.
Vex is old-fashioned and suggests worry as well as annoyance; irk is only mild annoyance.
Rile means to make someone angry and stirred up; irk is smaller and quieter.

sense: action that makes up for a wrong
definition: Action taken to make up for a wrong or a sin and show that you are sorry.
nuance: Atonement means making amends for something wrong you did. It is used in religion, law and ethics, and in everyday speech with a touch of humour. It is usually followed by 'for'.

examples.text: As atonement for lying to his sister, he spent the weekend repairing her bicycle.
The company offered to pay compensation as atonement for the damage caused by the spill.
In many religions, fasting is a form of atonement for sins committed during the year.
I did the washing-up for a week as atonement for forgetting her birthday.
The court accepted the offender's community work as atonement for the harm he had caused.
Literary critics read the old sailor's endless storytelling as a kind of atonement for his crime.

cloze.text: Yom Kippur, the Day of ___, is spent in prayer and fasting by Jewish communities worldwide.
In ___ for his earlier cruelty, the king gave half of his wealth to the poor.
She saw her years of volunteering as ___ for the mistakes of her youth, though no one had asked her to.

misuse.text: Getting into medical school was the greatest atonement of her life.
misuse.why: Atonement is making up for a wrong; reaching a goal is an achievement or attainment.

misuse.text: The victim made atonement for the thief's crime.
misuse.why: The wrongdoer makes atonement, not the victim.

synonyms.vs: Amends is everyday and often about relationships; atonement is formal and has a moral or religious tone.
Penance is a religious punishment accepted for sin; atonement is the wider idea of making up for wrong.
Reparation means payment or action to repair harm, often by a state or group.

confusables.note: Attainment means achievement of a goal or standard.

origin: From the phrase 'at one': atonement first meant being reconciled, made 'at one' again with someone.

definition: Showing signs that something is likely to go well; favourable for the future.
nuance: Auspicious describes beginnings, signs, occasions and omens that suggest future success. It is positive and slightly ceremonial in tone. Its opposite, 'inauspicious', is often used for a bad start.

examples.text: The team's five-nil win in its first match was an auspicious start to the season.
Historians note that the republic's first peaceful elections were an auspicious sign for its democratic future.
Sunshine on the morning of my driving test felt like an auspicious omen.
On an auspicious morning in spring, the merchants set sail with a following wind.
The chairman called the signing of the treaty an auspicious occasion for both nations.
The reign began under auspicious circumstances: a good harvest, a peaceful border and a loyal army.

cloze.text: Everyone saw the rainbow over the stadium as an ___ sign, a good omen for the match ahead.
In ancient Rome, priests watched the flight of birds to decide whether a day was ___ for a battle.
She chose an ___ day for the ceremony, hoping that good fortune would follow the couple for life.

misuse.text: The auspicious fire destroyed the whole village overnight.
misuse.why: Auspicious means promising good fortune, so it cannot describe a disaster.

misuse.text: He is an auspicious student who always asks clever questions.
misuse.why: Auspicious describes beginnings, signs and occasions, not people; use 'bright' or 'inquisitive'.

phrases: This was an auspicious beginning to...

synonyms.vs: Promising is everyday and fits people or plans; auspicious fits omens, starts and occasions.
Favourable describes good conditions in general; auspicious suggests a sign of success to come.
Propitious is even more formal and stresses conditions that favour success; auspicious stresses the good sign itself.

confusables.note: Suspicious means doubtful or distrustful; it only looks and sounds similar.

origin: From Latin auspicium, built on avis, 'bird', and specere, 'to look': Romans watched birds for signs of what would happen.

definition: Unclear and badly connected, so that it cannot be followed or understood.
nuance: Incoherent describes speech, writing, arguments and people whose words do not link together sensibly. A person can be incoherent from shock, anger or illness, while a text is incoherent when its ideas do not connect. In essay feedback it is a sharp criticism.

examples.text: He was so upset that his answer came out as an incoherent jumble of half-finished sentences.
The essay is incoherent: its second half contradicts the first, and the paragraphs follow no clear order.
Police said the man was incoherent and unable to give his name when they found him.
Rage made her incoherent, and the words tumbled out in a furious rush.
The committee rejected the proposal as incoherent, since its aims and its budget did not match.
Critics dismissed the theory as incoherent, because its central claims could not all be true at once.

cloze.text: The witness was so shaken that his statement was ___: scraps of sentences with no thread linking one to the next.
My feedback was that the essay felt ___, with paragraphs jumping from topic to topic and no logical link between them.
Exhausted and feverish, the patient muttered a few ___ words and fell silent.

misuse.text: Her incoherent argument was clear, logical and easy to follow.
misuse.why: Incoherent means confused and badly connected, the opposite of clear and logical.

misuse.text: He gave an incoherent shout so loud that the whole street heard it.
misuse.why: Incoherent is about confused, disconnected meaning, not volume; use 'loud' or 'deafening'.

synonyms.vs: Confused is general and can describe minds or situations; incoherent focuses on speech or writing that does not hang together.
Illogical means breaking the rules of reasoning; incoherent means the parts do not connect, so the whole is unclear.
Garbled describes a message distorted on its way; incoherent suggests ideas that were never well connected.

confusables.note: Inconsistent means not staying the same or contradicting itself; incoherent means too confused to follow.

origin: From Latin in-, 'not', and cohaerere, 'to stick together': an incoherent text does not hold together.

sense: too ready to give people what they want
definition: Too ready to give people what they want or to excuse their faults.
nuance: Indulgent describes people who spoil others or go easy on their faults. It can be mild and affectionate, as in an indulgent smile, or critical, as in an indulgent parent. Do not confuse it with 'self-indulgent', which means pleasing yourself.

examples.text: My grandparents are far too indulgent: they let the kids eat dessert before dinner.
Researchers found that indulgent parenting, with few rules and little correction, is linked to poor self-control in children.
Critics called the judge's ruling indulgent, since the fine was smaller than the money the company had saved by breaking the law.
The old teacher gave the noisy class an indulgent smile and let them finish their game.
The review warned that the university had been indulgent towards departments that regularly overspent.
Historians describe the old king as an indulgent father who forgave his sons every rebellion, until one of them took his throne.

cloze.text: Parents who are too ___ give their children everything they ask for and rarely say no.
Grandparents are often ___, spoiling the children with sweets and late bedtimes that the parents would never allow.
Her uncle, who loved to spoil her, watched the toddler's mess with an ___ smile.

misuse.text: The indulgent teacher punished every mistake with detention.
misuse.why: Indulgent means too ready to excuse or allow things, so harsh punishment is the opposite.

misuse.text: She is deeply indulgent in charity work and volunteers every weekend.
misuse.why: Indulgent means too ready to give people what they want; for being busy with something, use 'involved'.

synonyms.vs: Lenient is about being mild in punishing or judging; indulgent is about giving people what they want.
Permissive describes relaxed rules, often in a social or moral sense; indulgent adds the idea of spoiling.
Tolerant accepts differences calmly; indulgent gives in to wishes, sometimes too much.

confusables.note: Indigent means very poor.

definition: The ability to judge situations quickly and accurately, especially in business or politics.
nuance: Acumen is always approving and is usually followed by a field: business acumen, political acumen. It suggests a sharp, practical mind that sees opportunities and dangers early. It is uncountable, so we say 'her acumen', not 'an acumen'.

examples.text: Her business acumen turned a tiny shop into a chain of forty stores within ten years.
The study links financial acumen in early adulthood to better long-term savings.
You'd be amazed at his acumen: he spotted the flaw in the contract in about two minutes.
The old detective's acumen was legendary; he could read a lie in a person's hands.
The role requires strong commercial acumen and experience of managing large budgets.
Historians praise the minister's political acumen in building a coalition from bitter rivals.

cloze.text: Her financial ___ was obvious: she saw the market crash coming and sold everything just in time.
The firm hired him for his legal ___, his quick eye for the weak point in any contract.
Uniting bitter rivals into one government took real political ___: the sharp, quick judgement to see what each side would accept.

misuse.text: The gymnast showed great acumen on the balance beam.
misuse.why: Acumen is sharp judgement in fields like business or politics, not physical skill or balance.

misuse.text: She has an acumen for languages and speaks five of them.
misuse.why: Acumen is uncountable and means sharp judgement, not a talent; say 'a gift for languages'.

synonyms.vs: Shrewdness stresses cleverness in dealing with people and money; acumen is a more formal word for sharp judgement in a field.
Insight is a deep understanding of something; acumen is practical skill in judging and acting.
Savvy is informal and means practical know-how; acumen is formal and sounds more impressive.

confusables.note: Acuity means sharpness of the senses or the mind, as in visual acuity; acumen is sharp judgement.

origin: From Latin acumen, 'sharpness' or 'point', from acuere, 'to sharpen'.

definition: Fair and impartial because you have nothing to gain or lose from the result.
nuance: Disinterested means free from personal bias or advantage, so it praises judges, experts, advice and research. Many people also use it to mean 'bored' or 'not interested', but careful writers keep the two words apart. In essays, use it for sources with no stake in the outcome.

examples.text: Because the arbitrator has no money or friends at stake, she can give disinterested advice to both sides.
Science aims to be a disinterested search for truth, free from the wishes of funders and politicians.
The inquiry will be led by a disinterested panel with no ties to the company or the government.
I'd like some disinterested advice, so I'm asking you, since you've nothing to gain either way.
He watched the quarrel with disinterested calm, as a stranger on a train might.
Readers should ask whether the author is a disinterested observer or has a stake in the outcome.

cloze.text: A juror must be ___, with nothing to gain or lose from the verdict and no loyalty to either side.
Unlike a bored listener, a ___ judge cares a great deal about the case but has no personal stake in it.
She offered ___ advice, caring only about what was best for him and not about what she might gain.

misuse.text: I was disinterested in the lecture, so I fell asleep.
misuse.why: Disinterested means impartial; for bored or lacking interest use 'uninterested'.

misuse.text: The disinterested judge owned half the company on trial.
misuse.why: A disinterested judge has no personal stake, but owning the company is exactly a stake.

synonyms.vs: Impartial stresses treating all sides equally; disinterested stresses having no personal stake in the result.
Neutral means taking no side, often in a conflict; disinterested means you gain nothing from either outcome.
Objective is about judging by facts rather than feelings; disinterested is about having no stake.

confusables.note: Uninterested means bored or not curious. Many speakers use disinterested this way too, but careful writers keep the words apart.

sense: too severe to be repaired or put right
definition: So badly damaged or harmful that it can never be put right.
nuance: Irreparable is used with damage, harm, loss and breaks in relationships. It is common in law, where 'irreparable harm' can justify a court order, and in news about disasters. It stresses that money or effort cannot undo the damage.

examples.text: The fire caused irreparable damage to the library, destroying books that exist nowhere else.
Overfishing can cause irreparable harm to marine ecosystems that never fully recover.
I think that argument did irreparable harm to their friendship; they haven't spoken since.
She knew at once that the vase was irreparable, scattered across the floor in a hundred pieces.
The company asked the court to block the sale, arguing that it would suffer irreparable harm.
Some historians argue that the war caused an irreparable break between the two communities.

cloze.text: The flood did ___ damage to the ancient manuscripts, which no restorer could ever bring back.
After years of lies, the harm to their marriage was ___, and no apology could mend it.
A court may stop a company from acting if the action would cause ___ harm that money cannot fix.
