The coach was ___ with the late players, letting them off without any penalty at all.
Strict teachers enforce every rule, while more ___ ones often let small mistakes pass.

misuse.text: The lenient prison guard locked every cell and punished any small mistake.
misuse.why: Lenient means mild and forgiving, so strict punishment for small mistakes is the opposite.

misuse.text: The weather was lenient all week, so we had a picnic every day.
misuse.why: Lenient describes people, rules or punishments that are not strict; for weather, say 'mild'.

synonyms.vs: Merciful stresses compassion shown to someone at your mercy; lenient is about being less strict in applying rules or punishments.
Tolerant means accepting different views or behaviour; lenient means being soft on rule-breaking.
Indulgent means giving too much of what someone wants; lenient means punishing or demanding less.

origin: From Latin lenire, 'to soften or soothe', from lenis, 'soft'.

sense: moving from place to place as a way of life
definition: Moving from place to place rather than living in one settled home.
nuance: Nomadic describes peoples, herders and lifestyles that move regularly, usually following food, water or grazing land. It is neutral in history and anthropology. It can also describe modern workers who change place often.

examples.text: The nomadic herders move their sheep to new pastures each season and live in tents.
Anthropologists study how nomadic communities adapt their routes to changing climates.
I've had a pretty nomadic life since graduating: three cities and five flats in four years.
The ministry supports schooling for the children of nomadic families.
The nomadic tribe packed its tents at dawn and vanished into the desert.
A nomadic way of life gave way to farming as people learned to grow crops.

cloze.text: Unlike farmers who stay in one village, ___ peoples travel with their animals in search of fresh grass.
After a ___ childhood spent in six countries, she never felt tied to a single hometown.
The tribe lived a ___ life, packing up their tents whenever the water ran low.

misuse.text: The nomadic farmer lived in the same house all his life and never left his village.
misuse.why: Nomadic means moving from place to place, so staying in one house all his life is the opposite.

misuse.text: The nomadic geese fly south every autumn and return in spring.
misuse.why: For animals that move between regions each season, the usual word is 'migratory'; nomadic is mostly used for people.

synonyms.vs: Wandering is everyday and can be aimless; nomadic suggests a regular pattern of movement, often seasonal, for a way of life.
Itinerant describes people who travel from place to place for work; nomadic describes whole peoples and lifestyles.
Migratory is usually used for animals moving between regions; nomadic is mostly used for humans.

origin: From Greek nomas, 'roaming in search of pasture'.

sense: so absurd it is almost laughable
definition: So absurd and unreasonable that it is almost laughable.
nuance: Preposterous is a strong word for ideas, claims and demands that are completely unreasonable or silly. It is critical and often a little scornful, and is common in speech as well as writing. In essays, use it sparingly: 'implausible' sounds more measured.

examples.text: Mum said the idea of paying fifty pounds for a plain T-shirt was preposterous.
Early critics dismissed the theory as preposterous, yet later experiments supported it.
The minister called the allegations preposterous and demanded an apology.
It would be preposterous to suggest that one small error caused the whole collapse.
She burst out laughing at the preposterous costume he had made from cardboard and foil.
The author uses preposterous scenarios to show how fragile our assumptions are.

cloze.text: The claim that a goldfish could run the company was not merely absurd but utterly ___, and the whole room burst out laughing.
Tickets cost a ___ amount of money, more than a month's rent, and people simply laughed.
It is ___ to expect one person to do the work of twenty, and the manager knew it.

misuse.text: The preposterous teacher gave clear, sensible advice that helped everyone.
misuse.why: Preposterous means absurd, which clashes with clear, sensible advice.

misuse.text: Thanks to its oil exports, the country became preposterous in the 1970s.
misuse.why: This confuses preposterous with prosperous; preposterous means absurd.

synonyms.vs: Absurd is more general and may be mild; preposterous is stronger and suggests an idea is utterly unreasonable.
Ridiculous is everyday and can mean silly in a harmless way; preposterous is more formal and sharply critical.
Outlandish means strange and unconventional; preposterous means so unreasonable it cannot be taken seriously.

confusables.note: Prosperous means rich and successful.

origin: From Latin praeposterus, 'before-after', meaning back to front, which developed into 'absurd'.

sense: favouring a privileged few over everyone else
definition: Believing that a small, privileged group is superior and deserves more power or advantages than others.
nuance: Elitist describes people, attitudes, systems and institutions that favour a select few, such as the rich or highly educated. It is almost always critical, often an accusation in debates about education, culture and politics. It is also a noun: 'an elitist'.

examples.text: Critics called the golf club elitist because membership cost thousands and new members needed two wealthy sponsors.
Some historians argue that early voting laws were elitist, giving power only to men who owned property.
It's a bit elitist to say pop music isn't real music, don't you think?
The university has pledged to reform its elitist admissions process and widen access for state-school pupils.
Her elitist parents were horrified when she announced that she was leaving university to become a plumber.
The author rejects the elitist view that only trained experts can judge great art.

cloze.text: Not just snobbish but openly ___, the club's leaders believed a privileged few should run the whole town.
Critics say the scheme is ___, designed by a privileged minority to benefit people like themselves and shut others out.
Populists attack the ___ attitudes of experts who, they say, think only a select few are fit to make decisions.

misuse.text: The school is very elitist: anyone can join, and it is free for every child.
misuse.why: Elitist means favouring a privileged few; open, free entry for everyone is the opposite.

misuse.text: She is an elitist tennis player and has won every match this year.
misuse.why: This confuses elitist with elite; an elite player is top-level, while elitist is about attitudes to privilege.

synonyms.vs: Snobbish is everyday and about looking down on others' taste or class; elitist is about believing a select group deserves power or privilege.
Exclusive can be neutral or approving (an exclusive resort); elitist is critical and points to unfair privilege.
Highbrow describes demanding, intellectual culture and can be neutral; elitist criticises looking down on people who prefer something else.

confusables.note: As an adjective, elite means top-level or the best (elite athletes), with no criticism.

origin: From elite, French for 'chosen', from elire, 'to choose'.

sense: being widely known for something shameful
definition: The state of being widely known for something shameful or wicked.
nuance: Infamy is public fame for something shameful, such as a crime, betrayal or disaster. It is formal and strong, and often has a historical or dramatic ring. Unlike 'fame', it is always negative; 'notoriety' is close in meaning but a little milder.

examples.text: The general earned lasting infamy for burning the city and betraying his own allies.
Few events in the war gained such infamy as the burning of the library.
That restaurant has a certain infamy in town after the health inspector shut it down.
The scandal brought the firm lasting infamy, and its name is still used as a warning in business schools.
He had hoped for glory but found only infamy, and children whispered his name in fear.
The ship's name passed into infamy after the mutiny, and historians still argue about who was to blame.

cloze.text: The prison camp's name has passed into ___: everyone knows it, but only for the horrors done there.
The date of the attack became a day of national ___, remembered with shame and anger.
Fame can be good or bad, but ___ is always the shameful kind, earned by wicked deeds.

misuse.text: She achieved great infamy by winning the Nobel Prize for her research.
misuse.why: Infamy is a shameful reputation; a prize brings honour, not infamy.

misuse.text: The infamy of the village is its lovely harvest festival, which draws visitors every year.
misuse.why: Infamy means a bad reputation, so a lovely festival brings fame, not infamy.

synonyms.vs: Notoriety is close and more common; infamy is stronger and often carries historic weight or moral disgust.
Disgrace is losing respect, privately or publicly; infamy is wide, lasting public knowledge of the shame.
Dishonour is loss of honour; infamy adds that everyone knows about it.

confusables.note: Infancy means early childhood or the early stage of something.

origin: From Latin infamia, 'ill repute', from fama, 'reputation'.

definition: Newly formed or just starting out, and not yet fully developed or experienced.
nuance: Fledgling describes new organisations, businesses, democracies and talents that are still growing. It often hints at promise as well as weakness, and it is common in news and business writing. It comes from young birds just learning to fly.

examples.text: The fledgling company had only three employees and worked from a spare bedroom.
The fledgling democracy faced great challenges as it tried to build trusted institutions.
I'm a fledgling writer, so please be gentle when you read my first story.
The foundation offers small grants to fledgling charities in their first two years.
The fledgling magician fumbled his cards while the crowd waited.
Economists argue that fledgling industries may need protection from foreign competition.

cloze.text: Like young birds just learning to fly, many ___ businesses crash in their first year because they have little money and no track record.
The country's ___ democracy, still finding its wings after decades of dictatorship, had fragile institutions.
Small grants help ___ artists, just out of the nest of art school, who have no reputation yet.

misuse.text: The fledgling professor had taught for forty years and written fifty books.
misuse.why: Fledgling means new and inexperienced, which contradicts forty years of teaching.

misuse.text: Sales were fledgling, falling every month as customers lost interest.
misuse.why: This confuses fledgling with flagging; fledgling means new and still developing, not weakening.

synonyms.vs: New is plain; fledgling adds that something is still growing and not yet proven.
Budding suggests early promise in a person or talent; fledgling can suggest early weakness too.
Emerging says something is just coming into view; fledgling stresses youth and inexperience.

confusables.note: Flagging means becoming tired or weaker.

origin: From 'fledge', to grow the feathers needed to fly: a fledgling is a young bird just learning to fly.

sense: free people from legal or social restrictions
definition: To free someone from legal, social or political restrictions, especially slavery or unequal treatment.
nuance: Emancipate is a formal verb for freeing groups of people from slavery, legal control or unequal rights. It is common in history, law and politics writing, and it can also be used figuratively. It has a positive tone and often appears in the passive.

examples.text: The new law emancipated the enslaved workers, giving them freedom and the right to own property.
Historians debate how far the reforms truly emancipated women from legal dependence on their husbands.
Getting a washing machine emancipated my grandmother from hours of hard work every week.
The treaty sought to emancipate the colony from foreign rule.
He dreamed of emancipating his family from the debts that bound them to the landlord.
Education has often been described as a force that emancipates the poor from limited futures.

cloze.text: The act did more than free them in practice; it was meant to ___ the enslaved people in law, ending their legal ownership by others.
Reformers fought to ___ women from laws that denied them votes, property and a say in their own lives.
Once legally ___ from the old restrictions, the villagers were allowed to leave the estate and choose their own work.

misuse.text: After weeks without food, the stray dog looked badly emancipated.
misuse.why: This confuses emancipated with emaciated, which means very thin from hunger or illness.

misuse.text: She emancipated her old coat to the charity shop.
misuse.why: Emancipate is about freeing people from control; for giving things away use 'donate'.

synonyms.vs: Liberate is wider and includes freeing places from enemies; emancipate stresses freeing people from legal or social restrictions.
Free is everyday and general; emancipate is formal and used for groups held in legal or social bondage.
Manumit is a rare, formal word for freeing an enslaved person; emancipate covers wider groups and general freedom.

confusables.note: Emaciate means to make very thin through hunger or illness.

origin: From Latin emancipare, 'to free from ownership', built from manus, 'hand', and capere, 'to take'.

sense: something that came before and led to a later thing
definition: Something or someone that came before and helped prepare the way for a later, similar thing.
nuance: Forerunner is used for earlier versions, ideas and people that point towards something later, such as the forerunner of the modern bicycle. It is common in history, science and technology writing. It suggests a clear link to what followed, not just something older.

examples.text: The telegraph was a forerunner of the modern phone, carrying messages across long distances.
Experts see the town's trial scheme as the forerunner of a national programme.
My gran's old typewriter was the forerunner of my laptop, I suppose.
This agreement was a forerunner of the wider treaty signed years later.
The distant rumble was a forerunner of the storm that would soon flatten the village.
Several scholars treat medieval guilds as forerunners of modern trade unions.

cloze.text: Early steam engines were ___ of modern trains, showing engineers what might be possible.
Like a messenger running ahead of an army, the small protest was the ___ of the much larger movement that followed.
The Roman roads were a ___ of today's motorways, linking distant towns across an empire.

misuse.text: The forerunner of the race crossed the line last and was disqualified.
misuse.why: A forerunner is something earlier that prepares the way for a later thing, not a runner in a race.

misuse.text: The new model is the forerunner of the old one.
misuse.why: A forerunner comes first, so the old model is the forerunner of the new one.

synonyms.vs: Precursor is more formal and common in science (a precursor chemical); forerunner is a little more everyday.
A predecessor held a role or position before; a forerunner points ahead to what came next.
A harbinger is a sign announcing something coming, often bad; a forerunner is an earlier version leading to something later.

confusables.note: A front-runner is the leader in a race or contest.

origin: Originally a person sent ahead as a herald, from 'fore' (before) and 'runner'.

sense: cold and unfeeling towards others' suffering
definition: Cold and unfeeling, showing no concern for other people's pain or suffering.
nuance: Callous describes people, remarks and acts that show no sympathy. It is strongly critical and used about cruelty through indifference rather than active hatred. It is common in news about crime, politics and business.

examples.text: The callous remarks about the flood victims shocked the nation and forced the minister to apologise.
The study finds that callous attitudes towards the poor often rest on the belief that people deserve their fate.
It sounds callous, but I honestly didn't feel sad when I heard he had lost his job.
The inquiry condemned the callous disregard shown by managers for the safety of their workers.
He gave a callous laugh as the old man struggled to pick up his scattered shopping.
Philosophers ask whether a callous person lacks emotion or simply ignores it.

cloze.text: Like skin thickened by rough work, his heart had grown ___: the victims' tears no longer moved him at all.
The landlord's ___ decision to evict the sick tenant in midwinter caused public outrage.
She was not cruel out of hatred, but ___: she simply did not care how her words hurt others.

misuse.text: The callous nurse gently held the patient's hand and spoke kindly.
misuse.why: Callous means unfeeling, so gentle, kind behaviour is the opposite.

misuse.text: His hands were callous from years of digging in the garden.
misuse.why: For hard skin the word is 'callused'; callous describes an unfeeling attitude.

synonyms.vs: Heartless is everyday and plain; callous is more formal and stresses a lack of feeling, often through indifference.
Cruel suggests causing pain on purpose; callous suggests not caring that others suffer.
Insensitive is milder and means not noticing others' feelings; callous means not caring even when you do notice.

confusables.note: Callow means young and inexperienced.
Callused describes skin that has become hard and thick from wear.

origin: From Latin callosus, 'thick-skinned', so a callous person has a hardened heart as hands have hardened skin.

sense: dominant power or influence over others
definition: Dominant power or influence of one country, group or idea over others.
nuance: Hegemony is used in politics, history and social theory for leadership that becomes control, whether by force, wealth or by shaping what people accept as normal. It is neutral but often critical. In cultural studies it can mean the dominance of one group's ideas.

examples.text: The country's military and economic hegemony in the region ended when rival powers grew stronger.
Gramsci argued that a ruling class keeps its hegemony by shaping the ideas people take for granted.
Three big companies have a hegemony over streaming, and honestly there's little real choice.
The treaty was meant to prevent any single state from gaining hegemony in Europe.
Under the queen's hegemony, no lord dared build a castle without her permission.
Scholars debate whether English now exercises a cultural hegemony over global science.

cloze.text: Gramsci used the word ___ for rule by consent: a ruling class leads by making its ideas seem like common sense.
From the Greek for 'leadership', ___ is what the alliance feared any single nation might gain over its neighbours.
Critics speak of American cultural ___: not rule by force, but the quiet worldwide spread of its films, brands and values.

misuse.text: The choir sang in perfect hegemony, every voice blending beautifully.
misuse.why: This confuses hegemony with harmony; hegemony means dominance of one power over others.

misuse.text: The two countries shared equal hegemony and neither ruled the other.
misuse.why: Hegemony means dominance by one power; equal sharing means there is no hegemony.

synonyms.vs: Dominance is plain and general; hegemony suggests leadership over many states or groups, often with some consent.
Supremacy stresses being the highest or strongest; hegemony stresses control or leadership over others.
Domination is more openly forceful; hegemony can work through influence and accepted ideas as well as power.

confusables.note: Harmony means agreement, or notes that sound good together.

origin: From Greek hegemonia, 'leadership', from hegemon, 'leader'.

sense: guided by high principles, often unrealistically
definition: Believing in high standards or noble goals, often without paying enough attention to practical limits.
nuance: Idealistic describes people and plans guided by lofty principles and hopes for a better world. It can praise sincerity and commitment, but it is also often used to suggest naivety about practical difficulties. It is the opposite of pragmatic.

examples.text: She was an idealistic young lawyer who believed the law could end poverty, though she soon met harsh reality.
A group of idealistic students launched a campaign to plant a million trees.
Early socialist thinkers were often idealistic, imagining communities free of greed and conflict.
Don't be so idealistic; companies care about profit, not about saving the planet.
The mission statement sets out an idealistic vision of schools where every child can thrive.
Critics dismissed the plan as idealistic, since it ignored the cost of building the new network.

cloze.text: The young volunteers were ___ and hopeful, convinced they could end hunger in a single summer.
Her plan to abolish all homework was ___: guided by noble principles, but blind to how schools actually work.
Hardened by experience, he laughed at the ___ dreams he once had of changing the world overnight.

misuse.text: The idealistic accountant refused to believe in any principle except cold facts and profit.
misuse.why: Idealistic means guided by high principles, so believing only in cold facts and profit is the opposite.

misuse.text: It was an idealistic day for a picnic, with warm sun and no wind.
misuse.why: Idealistic describes people and beliefs; for a perfect day the word is 'ideal'.

synonyms.vs: Utopian suggests a dream of a perfect society that is impossible; idealistic is milder and can be admirable.
Naive is critical and means lacking experience; idealistic can be admired for its principles.
Visionary praises bold imagination about the future; idealistic stresses high moral principles.

confusables.note: Ideal means perfect or best possible; idealistic describes people guided by high principles.

sense: the theory and philosophy of law
definition: The study and philosophy of law: what law is, where its authority comes from, and why it binds us.
nuance: Jurisprudence is the academic study of what law is and how it works, a formal term used in universities and legal writing. Lawyers also use it for a court's body of past decisions. Do not use it as a simple word for 'law'.

examples.text: She studied jurisprudence at university, asking big questions about what law is and why people must obey it.
The new professor of jurisprudence says her lectures will tackle questions such as whether unjust laws must be obeyed.
My cousin is taking a module in jurisprudence, which sounds scary but is basically legal philosophy.
Candidates must pass papers in contract law, criminal law and jurisprudence before qualifying.
Late at night the old judge read dense books on jurisprudence by candlelight, hunting for a fair answer.
Feminist jurisprudence questions whether supposedly neutral laws treat women fairly.

cloze.text: At law school, she took a course in ___, which asks what law is and where its authority comes from.
Alongside practical subjects like contract law, students take ___, the philosophy of what law is and why it binds us.
A classic question in ___, the philosophy of law, is whether an unjust rule can truly count as law at all.

misuse.text: The jurisprudence broke into the shop and stole several phones.
misuse.why: Jurisprudence is a field of study or a body of court decisions, not a person or a criminal act.

misuse.text: He was fined for breaking the jurisprudence about parking.
misuse.why: A single rule is a law or regulation; jurisprudence is legal theory or the accumulated decisions of courts.

phrases: A central question in jurisprudence is whether...

synonyms.vs: Legal theory is the plain description; jurisprudence is the established name for that field.
Law means the rules themselves; jurisprudence is the study or philosophy of them, or the decisions of courts.
Case law means past judges' rulings; jurisprudence is the theory of law, though lawyers also use it for a court's rulings.

confusables.note: Prudence means careful good sense; it shares a root with jurisprudence but not its legal meaning.

origin: From Latin jurisprudentia, 'knowledge of the law'.

sense: involving much sitting and little exercise
definition: Involving a lot of sitting and little physical movement or exercise.
nuance: Sedentary describes lifestyles, jobs and habits that involve a lot of sitting and little exercise, and it is common in health and science writing. It is neutral but usually implies a health risk. In history and zoology it can also mean settled in one place rather than travelling, a separate sense.

examples.text: Doctors warn that a sedentary lifestyle, with long hours at a desk and little exercise, harms health.
The study links sedentary behaviour in children to poorer fitness and weaker concentration.
My job is so sedentary that I get my steps in by walking to the printer.
Employers are encouraged to reduce sedentary time by providing standing desks.
The old clerk led a sedentary life, rarely leaving his stool except to sleep.
Researchers found that replacing one sedentary hour a day with light walking lowered blood pressure.

cloze.text: Spending eight hours a day at a desk and then on the sofa makes for a ___ lifestyle.
From the Latin for 'to sit', ___ jobs such as data entry keep people in a chair for most of the day.
Health experts call long hours spent sitting at a desk and then on the sofa ___ behaviour.

misuse.text: The sedentary athlete trained for six hours a day and ran ten miles before breakfast.
misuse.why: Sedentary means involving little movement, so intense daily training is the opposite.

misuse.text: The doctor gave him a sedentary to help him sleep.
misuse.why: This confuses sedentary with sedative, a drug that calms you; sedentary is an adjective about sitting.

synonyms.vs: Inactive is plain and general; sedentary is a health term for lives and jobs with much sitting.
Stationary means not moving at a particular moment; sedentary describes a habitual way of life.

confusables.note: A sedative is a drug that calms a person or makes them sleepy.

origin: From Latin sedere, 'to sit'.

definition: Firm and loyal, refusing to change or give up even when it is difficult.
nuance: Steadfast praises people who stay loyal to a person, belief or purpose despite pressure. It stresses reliability over time more than 'resolute' does. It is formal and warm, often used for friends, supporters and principles.

examples.text: The team's steadfast supporters stayed in the rain to cheer them on after the defeat.
The author remains steadfast in her belief that education can reduce inequality.
You've been a steadfast friend through all this, and I'll never forget it.
The ministry thanked its steadfast volunteers for their loyalty throughout the long crisis.
The steadfast old dog waited at the station every evening for his owner.
Despite pressure, the committee was steadfast in applying the same rules to everyone.

cloze.text: Fixed in place like an anchor, her loyalty stayed ___: she stood by her friend even after everyone else turned against him.
The village's ___ support for the school, year after year, finally saved it from closing.
Not just determined but loyal and unwavering for forty years, he was a ___ ally who never abandoned the cause.

misuse.text: He was steadfast in changing his mind every five minutes.
misuse.why: Steadfast means firm and unchanging, so changing your mind constantly is the opposite.

misuse.text: She was steadfast to finish the race, so she ran faster than ever.
misuse.why: Steadfast is not followed by 'to' and a verb; say 'determined to finish', or 'steadfast in her aim'.

synonyms.vs: Loyal is everyday and about allegiance; steadfast also stresses not wavering under pressure.
Resolute is about firm purpose in action; steadfast adds long-lasting loyalty and constancy.
Staunch is very similar and often describes supporters; steadfast sounds slightly more formal and calm.

origin: From Old English stedefaest, 'firmly fixed in place'.

definition: Calm and peaceful, without noise, worry or disturbance.
nuance: Tranquil describes places, scenes and states of mind that are quiet and undisturbed. It is a positive, slightly literary word, common in travel writing and fiction. The noun is spelled tranquillity in British English and tranquility in American English.

examples.text: We rented a cottage by a tranquil lake, where the only sound was birdsong.
Studies suggest that tranquil natural settings lower stress levels in hospital patients.
The usually tranquil village was shaken by news of the robbery.
I love how tranquil the library is on Sunday mornings.
The hotel offers guests a tranquil garden for rest and reflection.
Her face was tranquil, and nobody guessed that a storm raged in her mind.

cloze.text: After a noisy week in the city, she longed for somewhere calm, quiet and ___, a lake where nothing disturbed the peace.
The sea was so ___ that it looked like glass, with not a single wave in sight.
Monks chose a remote and ___ valley, far from traffic, crowds and any disturbance.

misuse.text: The tranquil crowd screamed and pushed through the doors in panic.
misuse.why: Tranquil means calm and undisturbed, so screaming and panic are the opposite.

misuse.text: The vet gave the horse a tranquil before the operation.
misuse.why: The calming drug is a tranquilliser; tranquil is an adjective meaning calm and peaceful.

synonyms.vs: Calm is everyday and general; tranquil is more literary and stresses deep peace and quiet.
Serene adds a feeling of bright, graceful peace; tranquil stresses quiet and absence of disturbance.
Placid can suggest mild dullness or an easygoing nature; tranquil is more positive.

confusables.note: A tranquilliser is a drug that calms a person.

origin: From Latin tranquillus, 'quiet, calm'.

definition: Behaviour that is wrong, unsuitable or shocking according to accepted standards, especially in an official role.
nuance: Impropriety refers to conduct that breaks rules of proper behaviour, often in public life, finance or professional settings. It is formal and milder than 'crime': an impropriety may be unethical without being illegal. The phrase 'financial impropriety' is very common in news.

examples.text: The minister resigned after accusations of impropriety, including accepting expensive gifts from a company he regulated.
The study of public ethics examines how institutions guard against impropriety.
Mum says accepting free concert tickets from a client looks like an impropriety, even if it isn't.
The board denied any impropriety in the awarding of the contract.
In that strict household, laughing during prayers was a shocking impropriety.
Historians record numerous improprieties in the way the election was run.

cloze.text: An audit found no financial ___ in the charity's accounts: no dishonest or unsuitable use of money, only careless record keeping.
Officials who accept secret gifts risk being accused of ___ and damaging public trust.
The judge called the lawyer's private chat with a juror a serious ___, a breach of the proper conduct expected in court.

misuse.text: The impropriety of winning the lottery twice is extremely high.
misuse.why: This confuses impropriety with improbability; impropriety means improper conduct.

misuse.text: The minister was accused of impropriety for giving a long and boring speech.
misuse.why: Impropriety is a breach of proper conduct, such as misusing a position; a dull speech breaks no standard.

phrases: There was no suggestion of impropriety...

synonyms.vs: Misconduct is more direct and usually means breaking rules; impropriety is milder and may only be unsuitable.
Wrongdoing is general and everyday; impropriety is formal and suggests breaking standards of proper conduct.
An indiscretion is a careless or embarrassing act, often private; impropriety is a breach of standards, often in public roles.

confusables.note: Improbability means how unlikely something is.

definition: Not important or significant, and unlikely to have any real effect.
nuance: Inconsequential describes details, remarks and events that matter little and change nothing. It can sound dismissive, so it is useful when arguing that a factor can be ignored. It is more formal than 'minor' or 'unimportant'.

examples.text: The error was inconsequential: it changed none of the final results and nobody noticed it.
The minister called the leaked emails inconsequential, but voters disagreed.
Don't worry about the stain; it's completely inconsequential at a barbecue.
These differences are inconsequential for the purposes of this contract.
They filled the evening with inconsequential chatter about the weather and the neighbours.
Small differences in sample size proved inconsequential, so the authors pooled the data.

cloze.text: The typing slip was ___: it changed nothing in the results and led to nothing, so nobody bothered to correct it.
She tried to make polite, ___ conversation, chatting about the weather to avoid the real subject.
Compared with the main problem, the colour of the logo is ___ and can safely be ignored.

misuse.text: The inconsequential earthquake destroyed half the city and changed everything.
misuse.why: Inconsequential means having no real effect, which clashes with destroying half a city.

misuse.text: Her exam results were inconsequential: high one term and low the next.
misuse.why: This confuses inconsequential with inconsistent; inconsequential means unimportant.

synonyms.vs: Trivial suggests something silly or too small to bother with; inconsequential stresses that it has no effect.
Insignificant is close and more general; inconsequential stresses lack of results or effect.
Negligible is mostly for amounts or risks too small to count; inconsequential is for things that do not matter.

confusables.note: Inconsistent means not agreeing or not staying the same.

definition: The lowest or worst point of something, such as a career, a mood or a country's fortunes.
nuance: Nadir is the lowest point, after which things may improve, and it is the opposite of zenith. It is formal and common in history, sport and business writing, as in 'reached its nadir'. In astronomy it is the point directly below an observer.

examples.text: The team reached its nadir in March, losing ten games in a row and sitting at the bottom of the table.
The economy hit its nadir in the winter of that year, and recovery began slowly afterwards.
Eating cold beans from the tin on the kitchen floor was the nadir of my week.
Public trust in the institution reached its nadir after the scandal.
At the nadir of his despair, he heard a knock and found his sister at the door.
Historians mark the war's final winter as the nadir of the country's fortunes.

cloze.text: After a string of failures, the company's fortunes hit their ___, the very opposite of the zenith they had reached a decade earlier.
If the zenith is the highest point, the ___ is the lowest, the bottom of any fall.
His career reached its ___ when he was sacked, with no savings and no friends left.

misuse.text: Winning the gold medal was the nadir of her career.
misuse.why: A nadir is the lowest point, so a gold medal would be the high point of a career.

misuse.text: Sales climbed steadily to a record nadir this year.
misuse.why: A nadir is the lowest point, so a record high is a peak or zenith.

synonyms.vs: Low point is the everyday phrase; nadir is formal and suggests a dramatic bottom.
Rock bottom is informal and often personal; nadir is more formal and also used for institutions and periods.
A trough is the low point of a cycle, as in economics; nadir is the lowest of all, in any setting.

origin: From Arabic nazir, 'opposite', as the point in the sky opposite the zenith.

definition: Very small and disappointing, far less than is fair or expected.
nuance: Paltry is critical and describes amounts, sums, offers and efforts that are shamefully small. It often implies unfairness, as in a paltry wage or a paltry excuse. It is common in news and opinion writing.

examples.text: Workers who spend long hours in the cold earn a paltry wage that barely covers their rent.
The author dismisses the paltry evidence offered for the claim as too thin to support it.
They offered me a paltry five pounds for my old bike.
Critics called the compensation paltry compared with the damage that the company had caused.
He counted his paltry coins twice, hoping that somehow they would become enough.
Despite their paltry resources, the early researchers made several important discoveries.

cloze.text: The council's ___ offer of fifty pounds, insultingly small, did not even cover the cost of repairing the damage.
For such long hours of work, a ___ salary that hardly paid the bills was an insult.
Voters were angry that so ___ a sum was given to schools while huge amounts went elsewhere.

misuse.text: The paltry feast included roast beef, pies, cakes and wine for everyone.
misuse.why: Paltry means shamefully small, which clashes with a generous feast.

misuse.text: The farmer keeps paltry, mostly chickens and a few ducks.
misuse.why: This confuses paltry with poultry; paltry is an adjective meaning shamefully small.

synonyms.vs: Meagre is similar and less scornful; it just means too little, often of food or resources.
Measly is informal and contemptuous; paltry is more formal.
Trivial means unimportant; paltry means too small in amount, with a sense of shame or unfairness.

confusables.note: Poultry means farmyard birds such as chickens.

sense: the range of someone's authority or interest
definition: The limits of someone's authority, responsibility or interest; the area they are concerned with.
nuance: Purview is the range within which a person, body or subject has authority or responsibility. It is formal and common in law, government and academic writing, usually in 'within the purview of' or 'outside the purview of'. It is about scope and authority, not literally about seeing.

examples.text: Setting the school budget is outside the headteacher's purview; only the governors can decide it.
Questions of taste fall outside the purview of this study, which concerns only measurable effects.
Honestly, who I date is not within your purview, Mum.
Safety inspections fall within the purview of the regional health authority.
The magic of the old forest lay beyond the purview of the king's soldiers.
Literary studies once had a narrow purview, but it now includes film and games.

cloze.text: Decisions about court sentences fall within the ___ of judges, not of government ministers.
Whether the product tastes good is beyond the ___ of the safety inspectors, who only check hygiene.
The word looks as if it is about seeing, but a body's ___ is the range of matters it has authority over.

misuse.text: From the top of the tower we enjoyed a magnificent purview of the whole valley.
misuse.why: In modern use purview means range of authority or interest, not a view; for scenery use 'view' or 'panorama'.

misuse.text: Please send me a purview of the report before it goes to print.
misuse.why: This confuses purview with preview, an early look; purview means range of authority.

synonyms.vs: Scope is the general extent of something; purview adds the idea of authority or responsibility.
Remit is mainly British and means the task given to a person or group; purview is the area of authority itself.
Jurisdiction is official legal authority over a place or matter; purview is broader and less legal.

confusables.note: A preview is an early look at something before it is released.

origin: From Anglo-French purveu, 'it is provided', words that began parts of old statutes.

definition: Not controlled or held back, especially of strong feelings or behaviour.
nuance: Unbridled describes strong feelings and forces, such as joy, anger, greed or enthusiasm, that go without restraint. The tone depends on the noun: unbridled joy is positive, while unbridled greed is critical. It is common in news and fiction.

examples.text: The children screamed with unbridled joy when the school announced a surprise day off.
Economists disagree about whether unbridled competition benefits consumers or harms them.
The mayor warned that unbridled development would destroy the city's last green spaces.
Her unbridled enthusiasm for the project made the whole team smile.
The committee condemned the unbridled use of power by a handful of senior officials.
He threw his hat in the air in unbridled delight.

cloze.text: Like a horse running free with no reins, the crowd's ___ excitement burst out the moment the winning goal hit the net.
Critics blamed the crisis on ___ greed, with bankers taking huge risks and no one reining them in.
Not restrained in the least, the fans' ___ joy spilled onto the pitch after the final whistle.

misuse.text: She showed unbridled caution, checking every step three times.
misuse.why: Unbridled means without restraint, which does not fit careful, cautious behaviour.

misuse.text: She is still unbridled, though her sister married last year.
misuse.why: Unbridled has nothing to do with brides or marriage; it means not held back, like a horse without a bridle.

synonyms.vs: Unrestrained is plain and neutral; unbridled has more energy and suggests a wild horse.
Unchecked suggests something not stopped by any control, often a danger; unbridled suggests free, wild energy.
Rampant describes bad things spreading wildly, like crime; unbridled can be good or bad.

origin: From the bridle that controls a horse: an unbridled feeling has no reins on it.

sense: dryly humorous, with a mocking twist
definition: Showing dry, mildly mocking humour, often with a slightly twisted smile.
nuance: Wry describes humour, smiles and remarks that are dry, ironic and slightly mocking, often about a disappointing truth. It is quiet and understated, not loud or cruel. It is common in book reviews and descriptions of people.

examples.text: He gave a wry smile when he lost, joking that at least his socks had won.
The author's wry tone makes even grim historical events enjoyable to read.
The coach offered a wry comment about the weather after the match was cancelled for the third time.
She made a wry face when I mentioned Monday's meeting, as if we both knew it would be pointless.
The chairman's wry remark eased the tension at the long and difficult meeting.
Wry observations on office life fill the novel, from endless emails to pointless meetings.

cloze.text: She gave a ___ smile, her mouth twisted at one corner, as if quietly amused by her own bad luck.
With ___ humour, dry and a little rueful, he joked that his flooded kitchen was now an indoor pool.
The review praised the novelist's ___ wit, which pokes fun at its characters without cruelty.

misuse.text: The wry clown shouted jokes and laughed loudly at his own tricks.
misuse.why: Wry humour is quiet and dry, not loud and showy.

misuse.text: She felt wry after losing her keys and burst into tears.
misuse.why: Wry describes dry humour, not sadness or distress.

synonyms.vs: Dry is everyday and describes plain, deadpan humour; wry adds a twisted, rueful note, often in a smile or look.
Ironic means saying or showing the opposite of what is meant; wry is the humorous mood that often goes with it.
Sardonic is harsher and more scornful; wry is gentler and often rueful.

confusables.note: Rye is a grain used for bread and whisky; it sounds like wry.
Awry means off course or crooked.

origin: Originally meant twisted or bent, from an Old English verb meaning 'to turn'; a wry smile is a twisted one.

sense: a temporary departure from the normal
definition: A departure from what is normal, expected or typical, usually a brief or isolated one.
nuance: Aberration is used for a one-off oddity that does not fit the usual pattern: a result, a mood, a period of history. It often suggests the departure is temporary and will not be repeated. In science it also names a fault in how a lens focuses.

examples.text: The cold week in July was an aberration; the rest of the summer was hot and dry.
Historians argue that the dictatorship of the 1930s was an aberration, not the natural result of the country's past.
Her rude reply was an aberration; she is normally the politest person in the office.
The auditor flagged the sudden spike in spending as an aberration that needed an explanation.
He wondered whether the kindness she showed that evening was an aberration or a glimpse of her true self.
Odd readings can be dismissed as aberrations only if there is a clear reason to doubt the measurement.

cloze.text: One poor result in ten years is an ___, a brief departure from the normal pattern, not a sign that the whole school is failing.
The coach insisted that the heavy defeat was a temporary ___ from the norm and that his team was still the best in the league.
Compared with the long, peaceful decade before it, the riot that night looked like a strange ___ in the town's history.

misuse.text: Arriving late every single day became her usual aberration.
misuse.why: An aberration is a rare departure from the normal; something done every day is the norm.

misuse.text: I made an aberration in my maths homework, so I lost two marks.
misuse.why: An aberration is a strange departure from a usual pattern, not an ordinary mistake; use 'error' or 'mistake'.

phrases: This should be seen as an aberration, not a trend.
...was an aberration rather than the norm.

synonyms.vs: Anomaly is a neutral, technical word for anything that does not fit a pattern; aberration suggests a departure that is often temporary or regrettable.
Deviation is a neutral measure of difference from a standard; aberration implies something odd or wrong.

origin: From Latin aberrare, 'to wander away'.

sense: a ruler with cruel absolute power
definition: A ruler who holds absolute power and uses it cruelly or unfairly.
nuance: Despot is strongly disapproving. It describes rulers with unlimited power who oppress their people, and is sometimes used jokingly of a bossy boss or parent. Historians also speak of 'enlightened despots', who ruled absolutely but supported reform.

examples.text: The despot jailed anyone who criticised him and ruled the country for forty years without an election.
Some historians describe Catherine the Great as an enlightened despot who introduced reforms without sharing power.
My dad is a bit of a despot about the thermostat; nobody else is allowed to touch it.
International observers condemned the despot for ignoring every court ruling against him.
The village trembled whenever soldiers sent by the despot rode in, taking whatever grain they wanted.
Political theorists have long asked how societies can stop despots from seizing unlimited power.

cloze.text: The people finally overthrew the cruel ___ who had ruled them for decades without ever allowing a free vote.
Frederick the Great is often called an enlightened ___: he held absolute power but supported schools, science and religious tolerance.
Not a gentle leader but a harsh ___, he punished every sign of opposition with prison or worse.

misuse.text: The despot was loved by his people because he shared power fairly with elected councils.
misuse.why: A despot holds absolute power and rules harshly, so sharing it fairly is the opposite.

misuse.text: Every evening the buses return to the despot on the edge of town.
misuse.why: A despot is a ruler with absolute power; a place where buses or goods are kept is a 'depot'.

synonyms.vs: Tyrant stresses cruelty and abuse of power; despot stresses absolute, unchecked power.
Dictator is the usual modern political term, often for someone who seized power; despot is more literary and often used of rulers in history.
Autocrat stresses ruling alone with total authority and need not suggest cruelty.

confusables.note: A depot is a storage place or a small bus or railway station; it sounds similar but means something else.

origin: From Greek despotes, 'master of a household'.

sense: a closing section after the main story
definition: A short section at the end of a book, play or film that tells what happened afterwards.
nuance: An epilogue sits after the main story and often jumps forward in time to show how things turned out. It is also used for a speech to the audience at the end of a play. Its opposite is the prologue, which comes at the start.

examples.text: I loved the book, but the epilogue, which jumps twenty years ahead to show what happened to everyone, felt rushed.
In the epilogue to his history of the war, the author reflects on how the peace was lost.
The documentary's epilogue reveals that the factory reopened last year, saving two hundred jobs.
The paperback edition includes a new epilogue describing what happened in the two years after the trial.
In the epilogue, the old soldier returns to the village and finds the orchard in bloom.
Shakespeare's The Tempest closes with an epilogue spoken directly to the audience.

cloze.text: The last chapter ends the story, and then an ___, set ten years later, tells us who married whom and who went to prison.
Many novels open with a prologue and close with an ___ looking back from years later.
The film ends with a short ___ set twenty years later, mirroring the prologue that opened it.

misuse.text: The epilogue of the book introduces the main characters and sets the scene.
misuse.why: An epilogue comes at the end; a section that introduces the story is a prologue.

misuse.text: In my epilogue, I sum up the three main arguments of the essay.
misuse.why: An essay ends with a conclusion; an epilogue is a section after the end of a story, telling what happened later.

synonyms.vs: An afterword is a note about the book itself, often by the author; an epilogue continues the story.
A conclusion sums up an argument; an epilogue tells what came after the story.
Coda is a more poetic word for a closing passage, often shorter and borrowed from music.

confusables.note: An epitaph is the words written on a gravestone.
An epigraph is a short quotation placed at the start of a book.

origin: From Greek epilogos, 'the conclusion of a speech'.

sense: a story whose characters stand for ideas
definition: A story, poem or picture in which characters and events stand for ideas about morals or politics.
nuance: Allegory is used for works with a hidden second meaning that runs all the way through: each character or event stands for something else. It is common in literary and art criticism. Calling a work an allegory means it is meant to be read on two levels.

examples.text: Orwell's Animal Farm is an allegory: the pigs and horses stand for the leaders and workers of a real revolution.
The film is a simple allegory about greed, in which each character represents one of the seven deadly sins.
I thought it was just a story about a lost robot, but my teacher says it's an allegory about growing up.
Reading the old fairy tale again as an adult, she suddenly saw it as an allegory of her own unhappy marriage.
Medieval writers loved allegories in which virtues and vices appeared as people.
The artist's mural is an allegory of justice, shown as a blindfolded woman holding scales.

cloze.text: Every character in the poem stands for a human weakness, so critics read it as a moral ___.
On the surface it is a tale about farm animals, but beneath it runs an ___ about political power.
The painting is not a portrait but an ___ of peace: the woman with the olive branch represents an idea, not a person.

misuse.text: The scientist wrote an allegory of the experiment, listing the methods and results in order.
misuse.why: An allegory tells a story with a hidden meaning; a plain report of methods and results is not one.

misuse.text: The minister denied the allegory that he had lied to parliament.
misuse.why: A claim that someone has done wrong is an 'allegation'; an allegory is a story whose parts stand for ideas.

phrases: The novel can be read as an allegory of...

synonyms.vs: A parable is a short, simple story that teaches a moral lesson; an allegory is usually longer and has many symbolic parts.
A fable is a short story, often with animals, that teaches a lesson; an allegory carries a deeper meaning throughout.
A metaphor makes a comparison in a single phrase; an allegory extends the symbolism through a whole story.

confusables.note: An allergy is a bad reaction of the body to a substance; it sounds similar but is unrelated.
An allegation is a claim that someone has done something wrong, not yet proved.

origin: From Greek allegoria, 'speaking otherwise', from allos, 'other', and agoreuein, 'to speak'.

sense: the methods and theory of teaching
definition: The methods and principles of teaching, and the study of how best to teach.
nuance: Pedagogy is used in education research and teacher training for how teaching is done and why. It covers choices such as lectures versus group work. It is a formal word and is rarely used for casual teaching.

examples.text: Teacher training courses spend a lot of time on pedagogy, the study of how best to teach different age groups.
The school adopted a new pedagogy that replaces long lectures with group projects.
My maths teacher's pedagogy is simple: let us struggle with a problem first, then explain the answer.
Research in pedagogy suggests that frequent short quizzes help students remember more.
The ministry published new guidance on pedagogy in early-years education.
The headmaster scorned modern pedagogies and still taught every lesson by dictation.

cloze.text: Her research is not about what children learn but about ___: the methods teachers use to help them learn it.
The training college teaches both the subject itself and ___, the theory and craft of teaching it to young pupils.
Courses in ___ give future teachers the science behind their work: how children learn and which classroom methods help them most.

misuse.text: Our new pedagogy is very strict about homework and never accepts late work.
misuse.why: Pedagogy is the method or study of teaching, not a teacher; for the person, say 'teacher'.

misuse.text: He studied pedagogy to become a doctor.
misuse.why: Pedagogy is about teaching methods; a doctor studies medicine.

synonyms.vs: Teaching is everyday and covers the act of doing it; pedagogy is the method and theory behind it.
Instruction is the delivery of lessons or directions; pedagogy is the thinking about how best to deliver them.

confusables.note: Demagogy is winning power by appealing to people's fears and prejudices; it looks similar but is unrelated to teaching.

origin: From Greek paidagogos, a slave who led children to school, from pais, 'child', and agein, 'to lead'.

sense: a value far from the rest of the data
definition: A value or case that lies far from the others in a set of results.
nuance: In statistics an outlier is a data point far from the rest, which may be a mistake or a real but unusual case. Researchers must decide whether to keep or remove it. It is also used more widely for any person or thing that stands apart from a group.

examples.text: One house in the survey sold for ten times the average price, so it was an outlier and was left off the graph.
Officials said the single hospital with high infection rates was an outlier and not part of a wider trend.
Our school's exam results were awful one year, but that was an outlier; they're fine now.
The committee asked analysts to explain each outlier before accepting the overall figures.
The detective stared at the map: every victim lived near the river, except one outlier on the far side of town.
Outliers can distort an average, so researchers must decide whether to keep them in the analysis.

cloze.text: Nine of the ten test scores were close together, but one was far higher, so it was treated as an ___ and checked.
The scientists removed the ___ because a faulty sensor had produced a reading far outside the normal range.
On the scatter graph, one dot sat far from the cloud of others: a clear ___ that pulled the trend line upwards.

misuse.text: To find the outlier, add up all ten scores and divide by ten.
misuse.why: That calculates the average; an outlier is a single value that lies far from the rest.

misuse.text: She was an outlier on the committee because she agreed with everyone on every point.
misuse.why: An outlier stands apart from the group; someone who agrees with everyone fits in.

phrases: This result is a clear outlier, and...

synonyms.vs: Anomaly is any departure from what is expected; outlier is specifically a value far from the others in a set.
An exception breaks a rule or pattern; an outlier lies far from the cluster of results.

sense: courage to endure pain or hardship
definition: Courage and strength of mind that lets a person bear pain, loss or hardship calmly.
nuance: Fortitude is quiet, patient courage in the face of suffering or long difficulty, rather than bravery in a sudden danger. It is an approving word, often used of people facing illness, grief or hardship. In older writing it is one of the four cardinal virtues.

examples.text: My grandmother bore years of pain with such fortitude that most of us never knew how much she suffered.
The mayor praised the fortitude of residents who rebuilt their homes after the floods.
Medieval thinkers listed fortitude among the four cardinal virtues, alongside prudence, justice and temperance.
The award recognises the fortitude shown by volunteers who worked through the winter in difficult conditions.
It took all her fortitude to sit through the long night, waiting for news from the sea.
Studies of polar explorers often stress physical fortitude as much as technical skill.

cloze.text: Not a sudden act of daring but quiet ___, the strength of mind to bear pain patiently, carried her through three long years of treatment.
Climbing through the storm demanded great mental ___ as well as physical strength, because the suffering lasted for hours.
The nurses showed remarkable ___, bearing months of grief and exhaustion calmly and without complaint.

misuse.text: He showed great fortitude by running away from the dog as fast as he could.
misuse.why: Fortitude is courage in enduring hardship; running away in a panic is not that.

misuse.text: By sheer fortitude, she found a winning lottery ticket on the pavement.
misuse.why: Fortitude is courage in bearing hardship, not luck; 'good fortune' would fit here.

synonyms.vs: Courage covers bold action in the face of danger; fortitude stresses patient endurance of pain or hardship.
Resilience is the ability to recover; fortitude is the strength to bear a hardship while it is happening.
Perseverance means carrying on towards a goal; fortitude means bearing suffering calmly.

confusables.note: Fortuitous means happening by chance.
A forte is a person's strong point or talent.
Fortune means luck, or a large amount of money.

origin: From Latin fortitudo, 'strength', from fortis, 'strong'.

definition: Up to now, or up to the time being discussed, usually before a change.
nuance: Hitherto is a formal, slightly old-fashioned word for a situation that lasted until now and has probably changed. It is common in history and academic writing, often before an adjective, as in 'hitherto unknown'. It looks back from the present, so it needs a past or perfect verb.

examples.text: Hitherto, scientists had assumed the disease spread only by touch; this study shows it can also travel through the air.
Divers have discovered a hitherto unknown cave system beneath the lake.
Oh, a hitherto hidden talent! Why did you never tell us you could play the piano?
The captain, hitherto calm, suddenly shouted at the crew to turn the ship around.
The agreement removes restrictions that had hitherto prevented foreign firms from trading in the region.
The archive revealed a hitherto neglected group of letters that changed how historians view the period.

cloze.text: The museum's formal announcement described a ___ unknown portrait: until this discovery, nobody had known it existed.
What had ___ been allowed would henceforth be forbidden: the decree drew a firm line between past and future.
The new law lifts a ban that had ___ stopped students from working more than ten hours a week.

misuse.text: I will hitherto start my diet tomorrow morning.
misuse.why: Hitherto looks back to the time before now; it cannot refer to the future.

misuse.text: Hitherto, she is studying medicine at university.
misuse.why: Hitherto describes a past situation that has now changed, so it needs a past or perfect verb, not a present state.

synonyms.vs: Previously is everyday and neutral; hitherto is formal and implies that things are different now.
Heretofore is even more legal and old-fashioned; hitherto is more common in general writing.

confusables.note: Hither is an old word meaning 'to this place'; it is the first half of hitherto.

origin: From the old word 'hither', meaning 'to this place', plus 'to', so 'up to this point'.

definition: Very common or widespread, especially of something bad or unpleasant.
nuance: Rife is almost always used of unwelcome things such as rumours, corruption, disease or errors. It usually follows 'be' and often takes 'with', as in 'rife with errors'. It is stronger and more critical than 'common'.

examples.text: Rumours were rife in the village after the mayor disappeared for three days.
Early nineteenth-century cities were rife with disease because few had clean water or proper sewers.
Gossip is rife at my workplace; I swear everyone knows my business before I do.
The audit found that fraud was rife in the department's purchasing system.
The castle was rife with whispers of betrayal, and no one dared trust a neighbour.
Student essays on the topic are often rife with the same few errors in referencing.

cloze.text: Within hours of the announcement, speculation was ___ and every newsroom had a different theory.
Corruption was ___ in the old regime: it was everywhere, and almost every official took bribes.
The draft was ___ with spelling mistakes; there seemed to be at least one in every line.

misuse.text: The party was rife, so everyone enjoyed themselves.
misuse.why: Rife describes unwelcome things that are widespread, such as rumours or disease, not a pleasant event.

misuse.text: She felt rife of joy at the wonderful news.
misuse.why: Rife is for widespread unwelcome things and takes 'with'; it does not describe a person's joy.

synonyms.vs: Widespread is neutral and can be good or bad; rife is formal and nearly always negative.
Rampant suggests spreading out of control and is more vivid; rife stresses how common something is.
Prevalent is a neutral, technical word for common at a particular time; rife is more critical.

confusables.note: Ripe means fully grown and ready to eat or use.

definition: Useful or convenient for a particular aim, even if it is not quite fair or moral.
nuance: Expedient praises what works but hints that principle is being set aside: the choice is judged by convenience, not by what is right. It is common in politics, business and ethics essays. The word can also be a noun for a quick method.

examples.text: It was politically expedient for the minister to blame the previous government, even though he knew the facts were more complicated.
Machiavelli's The Prince is often read as advising rulers to do what is expedient rather than what is morally right.
Telling a little white lie was the expedient thing to do, but I felt guilty afterwards.
The board chose the expedient course of cutting training costs, which saved money this year but harmed the company later.
It would be expedient, he reasoned, to forget what he had seen in the cellar.
Critics argue that the treaty was an expedient arrangement that avoided war but solved none of the underlying disputes.

cloze.text: Cutting corners was ___ in the short term, saving time and money, but it was not right and it cost them later.
The mayor did what was politically ___ rather than what was fair, and everyone knew it.
Lying seemed the ___ choice, serving his immediate aim quickly and conveniently, though it was plainly against his principles.

misuse.text: Thanks to the expedient delivery service, the parcel arrived a day early.
misuse.why: Expedient means convenient for an aim, often at the cost of principle; for fast and efficient, use 'prompt' or 'expeditious'.

misuse.text: She was a very expedient friend who always told the truth and helped others at her own cost.
misuse.why: Expedient suggests choosing what is convenient for oneself, often against principle, so it does not suit a selfless, honest friend.

phrases: It may be expedient to..., but it is not just.

synonyms.vs: Pragmatic is usually approving and about realism; expedient hints at convenience over principle.
Convenient is everyday and has no moral edge; expedient suggests the easy choice may be improper.
Advantageous means bringing benefit; expedient means serving an immediate aim whether or not it is right.

confusables.note: Expeditious means quick and efficient.
Expedite means to make a process happen sooner.

origin: From Latin expedire, 'to free the feet', so to make ready or useful.

sense: formal forgiveness or freedom from blame
definition: Formal forgiveness for a sin or wrongdoing, or a declaration that someone is free of blame.
nuance: Absolution began as a priest's forgiveness of sins after confession. It now also means being freed from blame or guilt, often in discussions of responsibility. It is usually 'granted', 'sought' or 'denied', and 'no absolution for...' is a common way to say someone remains to blame.

examples.text: After confessing to the priest, he knelt and received absolution, and the heavy guilt finally lifted from his shoulders.
Medieval Christians believed that absolution, given by a priest after confession, cleared the soul of sin.
The inquiry gave the company no absolution: it found that managers had ignored safety warnings for years.
I told her it was fine, but she kept apologising as if she needed absolution from me.
The report refused to grant absolution to any official who had known about the fraud and said nothing.
Some critics argue that charity gifts offer wealthy donors a kind of moral absolution without changing how they earn their money.

cloze.text: Kneeling in the church, she confessed her sins and hoped the priest would grant her ___.
Giving money to charity did not buy the tycoon ___ for the way he had treated his workers.
The official report gave the ministers no ___: far from freeing them of blame, it named each one who had ignored the warnings.

misuse.text: The judge gave the criminal an absolution of twenty years in prison.
misuse.why: Absolution frees someone from blame or sin; a prison sentence is a punishment.

misuse.text: My New Year's absolution is to go running every morning.
misuse.why: A promise to yourself is a 'resolution'; absolution is forgiveness or release from blame.

phrases: The verdict amounted to absolution of...

synonyms.vs: Forgiveness is everyday and personal; absolution is formal, often official or religious, and clears blame.
A pardon is an official act cancelling a punishment; absolution frees someone from sin or blame.
Acquittal is a court's decision that someone is not guilty; absolution is wider and moral or religious.

confusables.note: Absolute means complete or total; it shares a Latin root but its meaning is different.
A resolution is a firm decision or promise, or the solving of a problem.

origin: From Latin absolvere, 'to set free', from ab-, 'from', and solvere, 'to loosen'.

definition: Going against the accepted beliefs of a religion or an established group.
nuance: Heretical began as a religious charge of false belief. It is now also used, seriously or playfully, for ideas that challenge a field's accepted wisdom. Whether it sounds bold or dangerous depends on the writer.

examples.text: The church condemned his teachings as heretical and forbade anyone to read his books.
Galileo was put on trial in 1633 because the Church considered his views on the Earth and the sun heretical.
Putting ketchup on a perfectly cooked steak? That's practically heretical in my family.
The economist's heretical proposal to abolish the central bank shocked his colleagues but won him many readers.
The committee dismissed the paper as heretical, since it rejected the field's most basic assumptions.
At the time, such heretical ideas about the nature of the soul could lead to imprisonment.

cloze.text: Medieval inquisitors hunted down anyone whose religious opinions were ___, that is, opposed to official church teaching.
For a lifelong vegetarian to praise a steak would be almost ___ among his friends, a betrayal of their cherished belief.
Colleagues called her theory almost ___, as if she had sinned against a religion, because it rejected the field's most sacred assumptions.

misuse.text: Heart disease is heretical in my family, so I have my blood pressure checked every year.
misuse.why: Something passed down from parents is 'hereditary'; heretical describes beliefs that go against accepted teaching.

misuse.text: He was praised for his heretical loyalty to the church.
misuse.why: A heretical view opposes accepted doctrine, so it cannot mean loyalty to it.

phrases: At the time, such a view was considered heretical.

synonyms.vs: Heterodox is a formal, neutral word for opinions that differ from the accepted view; heretical sounds stronger and condemns.
Unorthodox describes unusual, non-traditional methods or opinions and need not break any rule of belief.
Blasphemous means insulting a god or sacred things; heretical means going against official teaching.

confusables.note: Hysterical means wildly emotional or extremely funny.
Hereditary means passed down from parents to children, like a disease or a title.

origin: From Greek hairesis, 'choice': a heretic picks his own belief over the accepted teaching.

definition: Fixed for ever and impossible to change.
nuance: Immutable describes laws, truths, facts and principles that are fixed. It is stronger than 'unchanging' because it says change is impossible. In social science it often appears in the claim that something supposedly immutable has in fact changed.

examples.text: Many early scientists believed that the laws of nature were immutable, fixed for all time.
The president said the country's borders were immutable and could never be redrawn.
My mum treats Sunday lunch as immutable; the whole family has to be there, no excuses.
The contract contains no immutable terms; both parties may ask to renegotiate after one year.
To the old king, the order of rank at court was immutable, as fixed as the stars.
Sociologists reject the idea that gender roles are immutable, pointing to how much they differ between cultures and centuries.

cloze.text: Viruses mutate constantly, but the laws of chemistry they obey are ___: they cannot change at all.
Nothing in life is truly ___; even mountains slowly wear away over millions of years.
Scientists treat the speed of light as a fixed and ___ feature of the universe, the same everywhere and for all time.

misuse.text: Her immutable moods changed every few minutes.
misuse.why: Immutable means impossible to change, the opposite of moods that change every few minutes.

misuse.text: The wardrobe was so heavy that it was immutable, so we left it where it was.
misuse.why: Something that cannot be moved is 'immovable'; immutable means unable to change.

synonyms.vs: Unchangeable is plain English; immutable is formal and often used of laws or truths.
Permanent means lasting for ever; immutable says it cannot be altered even if people try.
Fixed is everyday and may only mean not changing for now; immutable means it can never change.

confusables.note: Immovable means unable to be moved, or unwilling to change one's mind.
Immune means protected from a disease or an influence.

origin: From Latin immutabilis, 'unchangeable', from in-, 'not', and mutare, 'to change'.

definition: So clearly true that nobody can reasonably argue against it.
nuance: Indisputable is a strong word for facts and evidence that leave no room for doubt. It is common in argument, law and sports reporting. In an essay, use it sparingly: calling something indisputable invites readers to look for an exception.

examples.text: Her talent is indisputable; even her rivals admit she is the best player in the league.
The fossils provide indisputable evidence that birds are descended from dinosaurs.
The video offered indisputable proof of where the car had been at the time.
The facts are indisputable, though the committee interprets their meaning differently.
It was an indisputable fact that the house had been empty for years, yet the lights were on.
Few historians would call the economic effects of the policy indisputable, since the data are patchy.

cloze.text: The DNA match left no room for argument: the evidence was ___, and even the defence did not challenge it.
That the Earth orbits the Sun is an ___ fact; no serious scientist questions it.
Her gift for music is clear and ___; even her fiercest critics admit it.

misuse.text: The indisputable rumour was repeated by people who had no idea if it was true.
misuse.why: Indisputable means beyond doubt; a rumour nobody has checked cannot be indisputable.

misuse.text: It is indisputable that some people prefer tea, but others may disagree.
misuse.why: If others may disagree, it is not indisputable; the word claims that no reasonable disagreement is possible.

synonyms.vs: Undeniable is commoner and often used of qualities (undeniable charm); indisputable is used more of facts and evidence that nobody can argue with.
Incontrovertible is more formal and often used of evidence in law and science.
Irrefutable is about arguments or proofs that cannot be proved wrong; indisputable covers facts generally.

definition: A person who is rejected and avoided by others, treated as an outcast.
nuance: Pariah suggests someone shunned by a whole group or society, sometimes unfairly and sometimes for wrongdoing. It is also used for states, companies and ideas that others will have nothing to do with, as in 'pariah state'. It is strongly negative about the person's status.

examples.text: After the scandal, the businessman became a pariah, and former friends crossed the street to avoid him.
Isolated by sanctions, the regime became a pariah among nations, cut off from trade and diplomacy.
Since I told the boss about the missing money, I've felt like a pariah in the office.
The new girl sat alone at lunch every day, a pariah before she had said a single word.
The company risked being treated as a pariah by investors if it ignored the new rules.
Studies of prison life show how pariahs, such as informers, are shunned by other inmates.

cloze.text: Nobody would sit with him or speak to him; he had become a social ___, shunned by everyone.
The country was treated as a ___ by its neighbours after it broke the treaty, and no one would trade with it.
After her betrayal, she was a ___ in the village, ignored in the shop and avoided at church.

misuse.text: The pariah was the most popular person at the party, surrounded by friends.
misuse.why: A pariah is rejected and avoided by others, so being surrounded by friends is the opposite.

misuse.text: Every Sunday the whole pariah gathered in the old stone church.
misuse.why: The people served by a local church form a 'parish'; a pariah is an outcast whom others avoid.

synonyms.vs: Outcast is more general and can be neutral or sympathetic; pariah stresses being shunned by a whole society.
Exile means forced to leave a place; a pariah may still live among those who avoid them.

confusables.note: A parish is a local church area and the people who live in it.

definition: To grow and develop quickly, becoming larger, more numerous or more successful.
nuance: Burgeon suits things that increase fast and in a healthy way: cities, industries, talent, populations. It is most often seen as the adjective 'burgeoning'. The tone is positive or neutral, though fast growth can bring pressure.

examples.text: The burgeoning tech industry has turned the quiet harbour town into a busy city of cafes and start-ups.
Nineteenth-century factories drew workers into burgeoning cities that struggled to provide clean water.
My little sister has a burgeoning interest in astronomy; she now has three telescopes and two posters.
The ministry expects the export trade to burgeon now that the tariffs have been removed.
In the spring the orchard burgeoned, and white blossom covered every branch within a week.
Research on the topic burgeoned after the discovery, and the number of published papers tripled within a decade.

cloze.text: In the warm spring weather the garden began to ___, putting out buds and new shoots everywhere within days.
The town's fast-growing, ___ population, which had doubled in five years, put heavy pressure on its schools and roads.
Since the film's release, her career has ___, with job offers arriving from three continents.

misuse.text: The village's population burgeoned as families moved away and the school closed.
misuse.why: Burgeon means to grow quickly; a shrinking population is the opposite.

misuse.text: She burgeoned her small business with a bank loan.
misuse.why: Burgeon has no object: a business can burgeon but you cannot burgeon it. Use 'expand' or 'grow' here.

synonyms.vs: Flourish means thrive and do well, without needing fast growth; burgeon stresses rapid increase.
Boom suggests sudden, often short-lived growth, especially in business; burgeon suggests steady, healthy growth and is more literary.
Proliferate means to multiply fast in number and can sound uncontrolled; burgeon is more positive.

confusables.note: Bludgeon means to beat with a heavy stick or to force someone into something.

origin: From Old French burjon, 'a bud', so to burgeon is to put out buds and grow.

definition: To teach someone a set of beliefs so thoroughly that they accept them without question.
nuance: Indoctrinate is disapproving: it means fixing beliefs in people's minds by repetition and pressure, not by encouraging them to think. It is used of schools, cults, regimes and sometimes advertising. Its opposite in spirit is 'educate'.

examples.text: The regime used schools to indoctrinate children, making them repeat slogans praising the leader every morning.
Critics argue that teaching only one version of history can indoctrinate pupils rather than educate them.
My parents never tried to indoctrinate me; they told me to read widely and make up my own mind.
Teachers are forbidden to indoctrinate pupils with any political or religious belief during lessons.
Indoctrinated since birth, the young soldier never questioned the orders that came from the tower.
Propaganda works by indoctrinating people with simple slogans until they repeat them without thought.

cloze.text: A good teacher helps pupils to think for themselves, whereas a propagandist tries to ___ them with fixed ideas.
The cult ___ its new members, repeating the same claims for hours until nobody dared to doubt them.
Children brought up in the sect were ___ from an early age, taught to accept its teachings without question and to fear the outside world.

misuse.text: The teacher indoctrinated the class by encouraging them to question everything.
misuse.why: Indoctrinate means drilling beliefs in without question, so encouraging questions is the opposite.
