misuse.text: The new members were indoctrinated into the club at a formal dinner.
misuse.why: Being formally admitted to a club is being 'inducted'; indoctrinate means filling someone with beliefs they must not question.

synonyms.vs: Brainwash is informal and stronger, suggesting force; indoctrinate is formal and often gradual, through teaching.
Educate is approving and encourages thinking; indoctrinate is critical and discourages it.
Condition suggests training someone to react automatically; indoctrinate is about fixing beliefs.

origin: From the noun doctrine, from Latin doctrina, 'teaching'.

sense: the highest point of success or power
definition: The highest point, especially the moment of greatest success, power or fame.
nuance: Zenith literally means the point in the sky directly overhead. In writing it names the high point of a career, empire, civilisation or trend, and it suggests that decline comes afterwards. It is common in the phrases 'reach its zenith' and 'at the zenith of'.

examples.text: The Roman Empire reached its zenith in the early second century, when its borders stretched from Britain to the Middle East.
Honestly, that tournament was the zenith of her career; she never played that well again.
At the zenith of his fame, the singer sold out stadiums in forty countries.
The company reached its zenith in 1999, then lost half its value within three years.
Looking back, he knew that summer had been the zenith of his life; nothing afterwards ever shone so brightly.
Many historians date the zenith of the Dutch Golden Age to the middle of the seventeenth century.

cloze.text: After years of climbing, the band reached the ___ of its fame, and then it split up.
From the nadir of defeat in 1940 to the ___ of victory in 1945, the country's fortunes changed completely.
Winning the prize was the ___ of her career, and critics wondered if she could ever do better.

misuse.text: After the crash, the firm sank to its zenith and lost all its customers.
misuse.why: Zenith is the highest point; the lowest point is the nadir.

misuse.text: They celebrated the zenith of the project at its very beginning, when nothing had been built.
misuse.why: Zenith means the high point reached after growth, not the start of something.

phrases: At the zenith of its power,...

synonyms.vs: Peak is everyday and general; zenith is literary and suggests a final high point before decline.
Pinnacle suggests the top of an achievement; zenith more often marks the highest point of an era or power.
Apex is a neutral, geometric word for the top; zenith carries a sense of the grandest moment.

origin: From Arabic samt ar-ra's, 'the path over the head', through medieval Latin.

sense: seize power or a place wrongly
definition: To take a position, power or right by force or without having the right to it.
nuance: Usurp is used of power, thrones, roles and authority taken unlawfully or unfairly. It is common in history and politics, and lightly when a cat takes your chair. The usual objects are 'the throne', 'power', 'authority' and 'the role of'.

examples.text: The king's brother usurped the throne while the rightful heir was abroad, and had himself crowned within a week.
In Shakespeare's Macbeth, the hero usurps the crown by murder, and the play shows the cost of that crime.
Critics accused the president of usurping the powers of parliament by ruling through emergency decrees.
The cat has usurped my chair; she sits there all day and hisses when I come near.
The new rules must not usurp the authority of local councils to set their own budgets.
Some historians argue that television usurped the newspaper's role as the nation's main source of news.

cloze.text: The general tried to ___ the throne, though he had no legal claim to rule.
Parents worry that screens ___ the place once held by family conversation at dinner.
A minister who ignores the courts and acts alone ___ powers that belong to the whole parliament.

misuse.text: The prince usurped the throne after it was handed to him lawfully by his father.
misuse.why: To usurp is to take power without the right; a lawful handover is not usurping.

misuse.text: A thief usurped my wallet on the crowded bus.
misuse.why: Usurp is for taking power, a position or a right without a claim to it; for stealing objects, say 'stole'.

synonyms.vs: Seize is everyday and works for anything; usurp is formal and suggests taking a position you have no right to.
Supplant means to replace, perhaps fairly; usurp means taking by force or without right.
Overthrow means removing a ruler from power; usurp means wrongly taking their place.

confusables.note: Usury is lending money at unfairly high interest.

definition: A person or thing that is a perfect or very good model of something and worth copying.
nuance: Exemplar is approving: it names the best or most typical case of a quality or type. In academic writing it also means a clear typical example used to explain an idea. It is formal; in everyday speech people say 'a model' or 'a perfect example'.

examples.text: The nurse was praised as an exemplar of kindness, staying long after her shift to comfort patients.
The novel is often taught as an exemplar of the detective genre because it follows every convention.
My grandfather was my exemplar of hard work; he never missed a day's work in forty years.
The school gave pupils an exemplar of a top-scoring essay so they could see what the markers wanted.
She was the exemplar of elegance, and every young woman in the room tried to copy her walk.
Researchers use exemplars, or clear typical cases, to explain abstract ideas to new students.

cloze.text: Held up as a perfect ___ of honesty, the judge was admired by lawyers and public alike.
For young cooks, the chef is not merely an example but a perfect ___, a model to copy: calm, careful and endlessly patient.
Students received an ___ of a top-scoring answer, a model to show the standard they should aim for.

misuse.text: Our captain tries to exemplar good sportsmanship in every match.
misuse.why: Exemplar is a noun meaning a model; the verb is 'exemplify'.

misuse.text: The exemplar was a rare insect found only in the north.
misuse.why: An exemplar is a model worth copying or a typical case, not a living specimen; 'specimen' would fit.

synonyms.vs: Model is everyday and wide; exemplar is formal and stresses a perfect, representative case.
Paragon is stronger and means a perfect example of a quality, usually a person.
Epitome means the perfect example of a type, whether good or bad; exemplar is mostly a good model.

confusables.note: Example is the everyday word for any case; exemplar is a formal word for a model worth copying.

sense: invent reasons to justify bad behaviour
definition: To find reasons that make a poor choice or bad behaviour seem sensible, often to avoid guilt.
nuance: Rationalise usually means making excuses to yourself: finding respectable reasons for something done for a less comfortable reason. It is a key idea in psychology; in business it can also mean reorganising to save money. British English spells it rationalise and American English rationalize.

examples.text: He rationalised buying a third pair of trainers by telling himself that the other two were nearly worn out, though both were almost new.
People often rationalise unhealthy habits by pointing to the one relative who smoked and lived to ninety.
The minister tried to rationalise the cuts as a way of protecting jobs, but few voters believed him.
It is tempting to rationalise a poor result after the event, but the review must look for real causes.
She rationalised her silence all the way home: it was not lying, she told herself, if nobody asked.
Psychologists describe how rationalising a decision afterwards helps people feel better about choices they regret.

cloze.text: Instead of admitting he was lazy, he tried to ___ missing the deadline, convincing himself with sensible-sounding reasons that were not the real ones.
It is easy to ___ a bad decision afterwards, inventing sensible-sounding reasons that were never in your mind at the time.
She ___ her overspending as 'an investment' so that she would not feel guilty about the bill.

misuse.text: She rationalised the cake by cutting it into eight equal slices.
misuse.why: To rationalise is to invent reasons that justify something, not to divide or share things equally.

misuse.text: He rationalised honestly that he had made a terrible mistake.
misuse.why: Rationalise means finding excuses to justify bad behaviour; admitting an error honestly is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Justify can be honest and sound; rationalise suggests the reasons are only excuses.
Excuse is everyday and about asking others to overlook a fault; rationalise is mainly about convincing yourself.
Explain away means dismissing a problem with clever reasons; rationalise stresses defending your own conduct.

confusables.note: A ration is a fixed share of something, or to limit supplies; it is a different idea from finding reasons.

definition: Friendly, pleasant and easy to get on with.
nuance: Amiable describes people, and their smiles, manner or talk, as pleasant and good-natured, without being intense. It is mild and warm, and can hint at a lack of edge or ambition. It is common in descriptions of character and in discussions that went well.

examples.text: The new neighbour was an amiable man who waved to everyone and always stopped for a chat.
Our dog is amiable with everyone; she would happily go home with a burglar.
The amiable captain chatted with fans for an hour after the match, signing every shirt they held out.
Reviewers described the narrator as amiable but unreliable, a pleasant companion who hides important facts.
The ambassador was amiable in private, but tough and unyielding at the negotiating table.
Dickens fills his novels with amiable characters whose kindness stands against the cruelty of the age.

cloze.text: Everyone liked the shop owner, an ___ man who greeted every customer with a warm smile and remembered their names.
Unlike his gruff, moody brother, Tom was easy-going and ___, the good-natured sort of person everyone likes to sit next to.
Her grandfather was an ___ old fellow, good-natured and smiling, happy to chat with anyone in the queue.

misuse.text: The amiable dictator ordered the arrest of his critics.
misuse.why: Amiable means friendly and good-natured, which clashes with harshly arresting critics.

misuse.text: After months of talks, the couple reached an amiable divorce settlement.
misuse.why: For friendly relations or agreements between people, use 'amicable'; amiable describes a person's nature or manner.

synonyms.vs: Friendly is everyday; amiable is a little more formal and suggests an easy, good-natured temper.
Affable stresses being easy to talk to, especially for someone important; amiable is about general warmth.
Genial suggests a cheerful, welcoming manner, often in older people.

confusables.note: Amicable describes friendly relations between people or groups, as in an amicable divorce; amiable describes a person's nature.

definition: Existing or happening at the same time as something else, especially in the past.
nuance: Contemporaneous links two events, people or records from the same period. It is common in history, law and science, as in 'contemporaneous records'. Unlike 'contemporary', which usually means modern, it needs a second thing to compare with.

examples.text: The two painters were contemporaneous, working in the same Paris studios in the 1880s, so their styles often overlap.
The court accepted the diary as contemporaneous evidence because it was written on the day of the accident.
Police released contemporaneous notes taken by the officer at the scene.
Wait, were the dinosaurs and early humans contemporaneous? No, millions of years separate them.
The letter was contemporaneous with the fire; the date on it was the very night the house burned.
The rise in crime was contemporaneous with rising unemployment, but this does not show that one caused the other.

cloze.text: The officer's ___ notes, written at the scene as events unfolded, were accepted as evidence in court.
The historian chose the word ___ rather than 'contemporary', which readers might take to mean modern: the two kingdoms simply existed in the same century.
Over the same summer, the rise in ice-cream sales was ___ with a rise in sunburn: both happened in the same period, though the hot sun was behind them.

misuse.text: She loved contemporaneous art, such as the paintings of the past year.
misuse.why: Contemporaneous means happening at the same time as something else; for art of today use 'contemporary'.

misuse.text: The contemporaneous events followed each other over the next decade.
misuse.why: Contemporaneous means at the same time, not one after another.

synonyms.vs: Simultaneous suggests exactly the same moment; contemporaneous allows an overlapping period.
Concurrent is common in law and computing for things running together; contemporaneous is used for periods of history and records.
Coeval is rarer and literary; it means of the same age or era.

confusables.note: Contemporary usually means modern; it can also mean 'of the same time', but contemporaneous only ever means that, so it avoids confusion.

sense: a vague feeling of unease or decline
definition: A general feeling of unease, weakness or dissatisfaction that is hard to explain.
nuance: Malaise covers a vague feeling of being unwell and, more often, a mood of discontent in a person, a group, a society or an economy. It is common in news and cultural analysis, as in 'economic malaise'. It is not a specific illness.

examples.text: I have a general malaise today: not ill exactly, just tired and flat, as if something is wrong.
Economists blame the long malaise in the housing market on high interest rates and falling confidence.
The poem captures the spiritual malaise of a generation that returned from war unable to believe in anything.
A strange malaise settled over the household after the funeral, and nobody could say what was wrong.
The survey found a deep malaise among staff, though no single complaint explained it.
Historians describe the 1970s as a period of national malaise, marked by strikes, inflation and loss of confidence.

cloze.text: After weeks of strikes and bad news, a heavy ___ hung over the country: a vague, lingering sense that something was wrong, though nobody could say what.
Falling morale, empty offices and constant complaints were all signs of a deeper ___ in the company.
The doctor found nothing wrong, but the patient still complained of a vague ___, a feeling of being unwell with no clear cause.

misuse.text: He tripped her up on purpose, out of pure malaise.
misuse.why: The wish to harm someone is 'malice'; malaise is a vague feeling of unease or dissatisfaction.

misuse.text: She felt a joyful malaise when she won the lottery.
misuse.why: Malaise is a feeling of unease or dissatisfaction, so it cannot be joyful.

synonyms.vs: Unease is everyday and can be brief; malaise is more formal and suggests a lingering, spreading mood.
Discontent is clear dissatisfaction with something; malaise is vaguer and harder to explain.
Ennui is a literary feeling of boredom and weariness; malaise includes anxiety and decline.

confusables.note: Malice is the wish to harm someone.

origin: From French mal, 'bad', and aise, 'ease'.

sense: travelling from place to place for work
definition: Travelling from place to place, especially in order to find work.
nuance: Itinerant describes workers, preachers, traders, musicians and teachers who do not stay in one place. It is neutral, though it can suggest a hard, unsettled life. It can also be a noun for such a person.

examples.text: Itinerant farm workers follow the harvest from one region to the next, rarely staying anywhere for long.
An itinerant knife-grinder arrived each spring, sharpening blades and trading stories for a night's lodging.
Medieval learning spread partly through itinerant scholars who travelled between monasteries and early universities.
My uncle led an itinerant life as a musician, living in a new city every year.
The charity supports itinerant teachers who bring lessons to children in remote communities.
In the eighteenth-century revivals, itinerant preachers carried their message from village to village.

cloze.text: The circus is run by an ___ company that packs up its tents and moves to a new town every week.
As a young man he worked as an ___ labourer, picking fruit in one county and building fences in the next.
As the daughter of an ___ preacher who moved from town to town, she changed schools almost every year.

misuse.text: The itinerant farmer spent his whole life on the same field.
misuse.why: Itinerant means travelling from place to place, so staying in one field is the opposite.

misuse.text: She gave an itinerant speech that went on for hours.
misuse.why: Itinerant describes moving from place to place, not speaking at length; for a speech that never seems to end, use 'interminable'.

synonyms.vs: Travelling is everyday and need not involve work; itinerant is formal and suggests moving from place to place for work.
Nomadic describes whole peoples who move with their herds; itinerant is more about individual workers.
Wandering suggests aimless movement; itinerant implies a purpose, such as finding work.

confusables.note: An itinerary is the planned route or schedule of a journey.

origin: From Latin iter, 'journey, way'.

definition: To officially clear someone of blame or guilt for something.
nuance: Exonerate is used when evidence or an inquiry shows that someone was not to blame. It is common in law, journalism and official reports, often in the passive: 'he was exonerated'. It is stronger than 'forgive': it says the person did nothing wrong, or much less than was claimed.

examples.text: New DNA evidence exonerated the man, who had spent twenty years in prison for a crime he did not commit.
The inquiry exonerated the pilot, finding that the crash was caused by a fault in the engine.
The camera footage exonerates him completely: you can see he was nowhere near the shop.
The review exonerates the early researchers, arguing that they could not have known the risks with the tools of the time.
Only the housekeeper's letter could exonerate her, and she had burned it years ago.
Defence lawyers rely on forensic science not only to convict the guilty but also to exonerate the innocent.

cloze.text: The new witness could ___ the accused by proving he was in another city at the time of the crime.
The report ___ the nurse of any blame for the patient's death, saying she had followed every rule.
He hoped the investigation would ___ him and restore his name after months of accusations.

misuse.text: The evidence exonerated the burglar, since his fingerprints were on every window.
misuse.why: Exonerate means to clear of blame; fingerprints on every window would prove guilt, not clear him.

misuse.text: Every summer the school exonerates its best pupils with prizes and certificates.
misuse.why: Exonerate means to clear someone of blame, not to honour or reward them; use 'honours'.

synonyms.vs: Acquit is a court's formal verdict of not guilty; exonerate can come from any inquiry or evidence and says the person was truly blameless.
Absolve is to free from guilt or blame, often morally or by authority; exonerate rests on evidence.
Vindicate proves someone or their view was right; exonerate clears them of blame.

origin: From Latin exonerare, 'to unload', from onus, 'burden': to lift the burden of blame.

definition: Happening in repeating cycles, so that the same pattern comes round again and again.
nuance: Cyclical describes processes, trends and histories that repeat in a pattern, such as seasons or booms and busts. In economics, 'cyclical' industries rise and fall with the economy. It differs from 'circular', which is about shape or about an argument that goes back to its start.

examples.text: Farming follows a cyclical pattern: planting, growth, harvest and rest come round again every year.
Economists describe the housing market as cyclical, with long booms followed by sharp falls and recoveries.
My motivation is totally cyclical; a month of working hard, then a month of doing nothing.
Steel and car makers are cyclical businesses whose profits rise and fall with the wider economy.
The old woman believed that history was cyclical, and that the same mistakes would return in every age.
Ancient calendars were often based on cyclical movements of the moon and stars.

cloze.text: The seasons follow a ___ pattern: spring, summer, autumn and winter, then spring once more.
Economists say that recessions are ___: good years and bad years keep taking turns in a pattern that comes round again and again.
Some thinkers view history as ___, a series of rises and falls that repeat over centuries.

misuse.text: His cyclical argument kept assuming the very thing it was trying to prove.
misuse.why: An argument that assumes its own conclusion is 'circular'; cyclical describes patterns that repeat over time.

misuse.text: The cyclical change happened just once and never again.
misuse.why: Cyclical change repeats; a single event is not a cycle.

synonyms.vs: Recurring says only that something comes back; cyclical suggests a regular pattern of stages.
Periodic means happening at intervals, not necessarily in a full pattern.
Seasonal ties the repetition to times of year; cyclical can have longer or irregular cycles.

confusables.note: Circular describes a round shape, or an argument that returns to its start; cyclical is about repetition over time.

origin: From Greek kyklos, 'circle, wheel'.

sense: the ability to prepare for the future
definition: The ability to see what will be needed in the future and to prepare for it.
nuance: Foresight is approving: it is sensible preparation for what is likely, not magic prediction. It often appears as 'lack of foresight' when a disaster could have been avoided. It is common in business, politics and planning.

examples.text: She had the foresight to pack umbrellas, so we stayed dry when everyone else got soaked.
Critics blamed the flooding on the council's lack of foresight in failing to build better drains.
Good policy requires foresight, since decisions about energy today shape the economy decades from now.
The founders showed remarkable foresight by saving a fifth of every year's profit.
Had he possessed a little foresight, he would have noticed that the bridge was rotten.
Historians have praised her foresight in training doctors before the epidemic began.

cloze.text: With ___ rather than hindsight, she saw the trouble coming and saved money long before the factory closed.
The disaster showed a complete lack of ___: no one had asked what would happen if the river flooded.
He had the ___ to book the tickets months in advance, before the prices rose.

misuse.text: With great foresight, she explained what had happened the day before.
misuse.why: Foresight is about preparing for the future, not looking back at the past; that would be hindsight.

misuse.text: After the eye operation, his foresight was so good that he no longer needed glasses.
misuse.why: Foresight is the ability to plan for the future, not the ability to see; here use 'eyesight'.

synonyms.vs: Forethought is careful thinking beforehand about what to do; foresight adds the ability to see what will probably happen.
Vision is a larger picture of the future; foresight is practical preparation.
Prudence means careful, cautious judgement about risk; foresight is anticipating what is coming.

definition: A major piece of work, especially a musical composition or a large piece of writing.
nuance: Opus names a work of art, most often a musical composition, and composers number their works (opus 27). 'Magnum opus' means someone's greatest work. It is also used with humour for a long piece of writing that someone is very proud of.

examples.text: Beethoven's Moonlight sonata is listed as opus 27, number 2, in the catalogue of his work.
My brother has been writing his opus, a fantasy novel of nine hundred pages, for six years.
The composer premiered her latest opus, a piece for choir and orchestra, in Vienna last night.
The catalogue lists every opus the composer published, from her first songs to her final symphony.
He spent forty winters on his great opus, a history of the valley that nobody would ever read.
Scholars treat the late quartet as the crowning opus of the composer's final years.

cloze.text: Composers number their works, so Brahms's first symphony is catalogued as ___ 68.
She called her sprawling final novel her magnum ___, the greatest work of her life.
In concert programmes, Beethoven's pieces are identified by their ___ number, which shows roughly the order in which they were published.

misuse.text: We went to the opus last night and heard a famous tenor sing.
misuse.why: A drama set to music and sung on stage is an 'opera'; an opus is a single work, often numbered.

misuse.text: He composed ten opus in his career.
misuse.why: Opus is singular; several works are 'opuses' (or the Latin 'opera').

synonyms.vs: Work is the everyday word for any creation; opus is formal and usually means a musical piece or a major work.
Composition covers any piece of music or writing; opus stresses a numbered or major work.
Masterpiece means an outstanding work; opus carries no praise unless it is 'magnum opus'.

confusables.note: Opera is a drama set to music; it is also the Latin plural of opus.

origin: From Latin opus, 'work'.

sense: different from the usual or traditional
definition: Different from what is usual, accepted or traditional, especially in methods or opinions.
nuance: Unorthodox describes methods, ideas and lifestyles that depart from accepted practice. It is neutral: it can be admiring or doubtful, depending on whether the result works. Unlike 'heretical', it rarely has a religious sense, and it is often used of teachers, doctors, managers and sports tactics.

examples.text: She has an unorthodox way of studying: she learns her notes by singing them in the shower.
The coach's unorthodox tactics, playing without a striker, baffled opponents and won the league.
Darwin's theory seemed unorthodox in his day because it challenged the widely accepted view that species never changed.
The surgeon used an unorthodox technique that was later adopted by hospitals across the country.
The headmistress, famous for her unorthodox methods, held lessons in the woods whatever the weather.
Few journals would publish such unorthodox views before the 1990s.

cloze.text: Instead of the usual textbook approach, the teacher used an ___ method and let pupils plan their own lessons.
His ___ lifestyle, living on a boat and working only in summer, puzzled his more conventional relatives.
Although the treatment was ___, breaking with standard medical practice, it worked.

misuse.text: The unorthodox method was the one every school had used for a hundred years.
misuse.why: Unorthodox means not following the traditional way, so a century-old method is the opposite.

misuse.text: The weather was very unorthodox for June, with snow on the hills.
misuse.why: Unorthodox describes methods, ideas or ways of living that break with tradition, not natural events; use 'unusual'.

synonyms.vs: Unconventional is the everyday word; unorthodox is slightly more formal and stresses breaking from accepted method or belief.
Eccentric is about odd personal behaviour; unorthodox is about methods or opinions.
Maverick describes an independent person who refuses to follow the group; unorthodox describes the way of doing things.

origin: From Greek orthodoxos, 'having the right opinion', from orthos, 'straight, correct', and doxa, 'opinion'.

sense: wander away from the main subject
definition: To wander away from the main subject while speaking or writing.
nuance: Digress is used of speakers and writers who stray from their topic, usually briefly and often before returning to it. It is not always negative: a digression can add colour. The phrase 'but I digress' is a common way to return to the point.

examples.text: Sorry, I digress; where was I? Ah yes, the train was late again.
The author digresses into a long discussion of music, which interrupts the argument but adds colour.
The speaker kept digressing into stories about his childhood, and the audience began to check their watches.
Please do not digress; the meeting must finish by noon and several items remain.
My grandfather digressed whenever he told a story, and each tale led to three others before the end.
Students who digress too often lose the thread of their argument and confuse their readers.

cloze.text: 'But I ___,' the professor said with a smile, as he always did when he noticed he had wandered off his subject.
To keep the essay focused, resist the urge to ___ into interesting side issues that are not part of your argument.
She ___ so often during the talk that the audience forgot what the original question had been.

misuse.text: He digressed his speech by repeating the same point five times.
misuse.why: Digress means wandering to another subject; repeating one point is not digressing, and digress takes no object.

misuse.text: The speaker digressed, keeping strictly to his topic.
misuse.why: To digress is to leave the main topic, the opposite of keeping to it.

synonyms.vs: Stray is everyday and covers wandering in general; digress is formal and about speech or writing.
Ramble means talking at length with no clear direction and is critical; digress means leaving the point, often briefly.
Diverge means separating into different paths or views; digress is about speakers leaving their topic.

confusables.note: Regress means to return to an earlier or worse state.

origin: From Latin digredi, 'to step away', from dis-, 'apart', and gradi, 'to step'.

definition: To accept something or agree to it without protest, although you may not really want to.
nuance: Acquiesce suggests reluctant or passive agreement, often because it is easier or because you have no power. It is usually followed by 'in' or 'to'. Critical writers use it for people who fail to resist something wrong.

examples.text: I didn't really want to see another action film, but I acquiesced because everyone else was keen.
The council finally acquiesced to residents' demands and agreed to close the road to heavy lorries.
Historians ask why so many ordinary citizens acquiesced in the new regime instead of resisting it.
The tenants acquiesced in the landlord's proposal, though they privately thought the rent was too high.
She sighed and shrugged; she would acquiesce, as she always did when her mother used that tone.
By acquiescing to unfair rules without protest, people allow them to become accepted as normal.

cloze.text: Most citizens disliked the new law, but they ___ in it, accepting it quietly without any protest.
After weeks of pressure from her family, she reluctantly ___ and signed the papers.
A leader who ___ to every demand soon finds that no one respects his authority.

misuse.text: The workers acquiesced loudly by going on strike.
misuse.why: Acquiesce means to accept quietly; going on strike is active resistance.

misuse.text: She acquiesced the offer with delight and shouted 'Yes!'
misuse.why: Acquiesce is passive, reluctant acceptance and takes 'in' or 'to'; eager acceptance is not acquiescence.

synonyms.vs: Comply means to obey a rule or order; acquiesce means to accept without objection something you may dislike.
Consent is willing, often formal agreement; acquiesce is more passive and reluctant.
Submit means to yield to a stronger force; acquiesce is quieter and may be a choice.

confusables.note: Acquit means to declare someone not guilty.

origin: From Latin acquiescere, 'to rest', from quies, 'rest'.

definition: To criticise someone severely and formally for something they have done.
nuance: Censure is formal: usually an official body such as a parliament, council or professional board states strong disapproval of someone's conduct. It is also a noun, as in 'a vote of censure'. Do not confuse it with 'censor', which is about removing material.

examples.text: Parliament voted to censure the minister for misleading the public about the cost of the project.
The medical board censured the doctor and warned that any further breach would lead to suspension.
Moralists of the period censured novel-reading as a waste of time, especially for young women.
The school censured him in front of everyone, and he's still embarrassed about it.
The old priest was quick to censure anyone who laughed in church.
Critics who censure the novel for its length overlook how much of the plot depends on those details.

cloze.text: The council voted to ___ the mayor for using public money on private trips, though it did not remove him.
The professional body decided to ___ the lawyer, placing a public record of its disapproval on her file.
The motion to ___ the prime minister, a formal statement of Parliament's disapproval, failed by ten votes.

misuse.text: The editor censured the article, cutting out all the political lines.
misuse.why: That describes censoring; censure means to criticise severely, not to remove material.

misuse.text: The report censured against the managers for ignoring the warnings.
misuse.why: Censure takes a direct object with no 'against': the report censured the managers.

synonyms.vs: Criticise is everyday and can be mild; censure is formal and severe, often by an official body.
Condemn is strong disapproval of something wrong, not always official; censure often means a formal rebuke.
Reprimand is a formal telling-off by a superior; censure can come from a group or the public.

confusables.note: Censor means to remove or ban material thought unacceptable.

origin: From Latin censura, 'judgement', from censere, 'to assess'.

sense: a stale, obvious remark said as if wise
definition: A dull, obvious remark, used too often, that is said as if it were wise.
nuance: Platitude is critical: it names a comfortable saying such as 'time heals all wounds' offered when real thought or help is needed. It is common in reviews and criticism of speeches. The speaker may mean well, but the remark adds nothing.

examples.text: All I got were platitudes like 'everything happens for a reason', when what I wanted was real advice.
The president's speech was full of platitudes about hope and unity but contained no new policy.
Good essays avoid platitudes, such as 'education is important', and make specific claims that can be argued with evidence.
The review dismissed the report as a collection of platitudes that told the committee nothing new.
He murmured a platitude about time healing all wounds, and she wanted to throw her tea at him.
Calling a complex problem a matter of common sense is a platitude that explains nothing.

cloze.text: Instead of real comfort, the visitor offered the usual ___ that 'time heals all wounds'.
The speech was a string of comforting ___ that sounded deep but were obvious, like 'together we are stronger', with no actual plan.
Marking essays, she circled every ___ that sounded wise but said nothing, such as 'life is full of surprises'.

misuse.text: His wise and original platitude changed how the whole country thought about justice.
misuse.why: A platitude is a dull, obvious remark; a wise and original idea is the opposite.

misuse.text: The new manager gave the team plenty of platitude to work as they liked.
misuse.why: Freedom to act as you choose is 'latitude'; a platitude is a stale, obvious remark.

synonyms.vs: A cliche is any overused phrase or idea, including in style; a platitude is an overused remark presented as wise.
A truism is an obviously true statement and may be harmless; a platitude is stale and used instead of thinking.
Banality is the dullness itself; a platitude is the remark that shows it.

confusables.note: Latitude sounds similar; it means freedom of action, or a position north or south of the equator.

origin: From French plat, 'flat': a flat, dull remark.

sense: a forceful one-sided attack in writing or speech
definition: A forceful written or spoken attack that argues strongly against someone else's beliefs or policies.
nuance: A polemic is a passionate, one-sided argument aimed at winning, not at weighing both sides. It can be praised as powerful writing or criticised as unfair. The usual adjective is 'polemical', and the word is common in book and article reviews.

examples.text: Her book is less a balanced study than a polemic against the education system, hammering one point on every page.
The columnist's latest polemic accuses the government of ignoring the countryside, and it has angered ministers.
Have you read his blog post? It's a full-blown polemic against homework, with no room for the other side.
The editor rejected the article because it was a polemic rather than a reasoned analysis of the evidence.
The pamphlet was a fiery polemic against the landlords, and men read it aloud in the tavern by candlelight.
Eighteenth-century polemics against the church often mixed serious argument with open mockery.

cloze.text: The article is not a balanced review but a one-sided ___ against the new tax, and it never mentions any argument in its favour.
Her book began as a calm study but turned into a fierce ___ against the whole industry.
In his pamphlet, a passionate ___ aimed at winning supporters rather than weighing evidence, he attacked every critic by name.

misuse.text: The polemic was a calm, balanced survey that gave equal space to both sides.
misuse.why: A polemic is a forceful one-sided attack, the opposite of a balanced survey.

misuse.text: There was a long polemic among the staff about the new timetable.
misuse.why: In English a polemic is one forceful attack on someone's views, not a dispute among people; use 'controversy' or 'argument'.

synonyms.vs: Diatribe is a bitter, angry speech or text, often abusive; polemic argues a case, even if one-sidedly.
Tirade is a long, angry outburst, usually spoken; polemic is more organised and usually written.
A manifesto announces aims and principles; a polemic mainly attacks opponents.

origin: From Greek polemikos, 'warlike', from polemos, 'war'.
